capabilities.capability: SkidDetector + odometry trust arbitration
capabilities.whyItMatters: Skid is the single largest source of odometry divergence, and it is exactly what makes a small team's auto work in the shop and fail on a real field with defense. 1690's algorithm is well known in the elite community and 135's Consul already ships it; nothing publishes it as a library. Detecting skid lets Rootstock automatically inflate odometry std-devs, favor vision, and (optionally) back off the setpoint generator — a genuinely elite behavior a small team cannot write themselves.
capabilities.prerequisites: Must be a Rootstock original implementation. The 1690 algorithm is described in a public 2024 software session video and reimplemented by others, but there is no canonical open-source Java reference to integrate — BUILD IT and document the math.

capabilities.capability: DriveInputStream — backend-agnostic driver-feel DSL (the good idea in YAGSL, freed from YAGSL)
capabilities.whyItMatters: YAGSL's SwerveInputStream is the single best driver-input API in FRC and it is locked to YAGSL's SwerveDrive. Reimplementing its builder shape over RootstockDrive means a team on CTRE swerve or AdvantageKit gets alliance-relative control, heading-lock, aim-while, translation-only, cubed axes and drive-to-pose for free — capabilities elite teams hand-roll every year.
capabilities.prerequisites: Note: REV removed the slew rate limiter from the MAXSwerve template because MAXSwerve 2.0 wheels no longer need it. Ship slewRate() OFF by default and document it as a traction band-aid, preferring TractionMode.SETPOINT_GENERATOR.

capabilities.capability: AlliancePerspective — one owner of the blue-origin convention, robot-relative vs field-relative, and the operator perspective
capabilities.whyItMatters: The alliance-flip trap is the classic small-team elimination-match failure: pose origin is always blue, but the DRIVER's forward is alliance-dependent, and resetting heading, flipping paths, and setting operator perspective are three different operations teams routinely conflate. CTRE already separates seedFieldCentric() (driver perspective) from resetRotation(Rotation2d) (absolute blue-perspective) and setOperatorPerspectiveForward(Rotation2d); nothing enforces the distinction across backends.
capabilities.prerequisites: None. This is pure convention enforcement and is the highest value-per-line item in the whole domain.

capabilities.capability: First-class differential/tank and mecanum parity behind RootstockDrive
capabilities.whyItMatters: The project brief explicitly targets small teams, and small teams run tank. Every competing option (YAGSL, CTRE swerve, AdvantageKit swerve templates) is swerve-only; only 135's unpublished Consul framework achieves tri-drivetrain parity. Shipping differential support that gets the SAME autos, the same vision fusion, the same replay and the same tuner is a genuine differentiator, and it is also the on-ramp: a rookie team starts on tank with Rootstock and changes one factory call when they buy swerve.
capabilities.prerequisites: Model on AdvantageKit's diff_drive template (DriveIO + GyroIO, Spark Max / Talon FX / Talon SRX, NavX or Pigeon 2, in-code kS/kV characterization, wheel-radius characterization, velocity PID, sim + replay). Do NOT build on RamseteCommand/SwerveControllerCommand/MecanumControllerCommand — all three are removed in WPILib 2027.

capabilities.capability: RootstockTuner — live, teaching-oriented PID/FF tuning for drive velocity, steer position and heading lock
capabilities.whyItMatters: The user explicitly asked for tuning software that teaches. Every existing option hides the loop (YAGSL) or dumps raw numbers on you (Tuner X, SysId). A tuner that shows setpoint vs measurement in real time, explains what each term did to the trace, gates you through a fixed order (kS -> kV -> kA -> kP -> kD), and refuses to let a student add kI to a velocity loop is something no FRC tool currently does.
capabilities.prerequisites: Requires the value-logging layer and mechanism visualization to already exist. Depends on AdvantageKit 2026 unit metadata for unit-aware graphing in AdvantageScope. Reuse Tuner X's Multi-device Control & Plot and Integrated Log Analysis (Beta, new for 2026) for CTRE-only teams rather than duplicating them.

capabilities.capability: Unified high-frequency odometry + sim backend selection
capabilities.whyItMatters: Measured: 50 Hz odometry gives mean error 0.388 m / std 0.180 m; 250 Hz gives mean 0.297 m / std 0.028 m — an 84% reduction in variance. That is the difference between an auto that works once and an auto that works every match, and it is invisible to a team that does not know to ask for it. Rootstock should make it the default, not an advanced option. Similarly, defaulting sim to maple-sim rather than CTRE's no-slip model means a small team's shop-tested auto behaves like the real field.
capabilities.prerequisites: NATIVE_250HZ requires a CANivore and Phoenix Pro for timesync; degrade to THREADED_100HZ automatically and log a warning rather than silently underperforming. maple-sim is delivered as template forks, so integration is manual work, not a dependency swap.

eliteTeamPractices: Run odometry off the main loop at 100-250 Hz with a dedicated thread and a lock. 6328's templates ship PhoenixOdometryThread/SparkOdometryThread with a `static final Lock odometryLock` (ReentrantLock) and ODOMETRY_FREQUENCY = 250.0 on CANivore, 100.0 otherwise; CTRE's SwerveDrivetrain does the same natively. Measured effect: 50 Hz -> 250 Hz cuts odometry std dev from 0.180 m to 0.028 m (84%) while mean error only improves 23% — elite teams optimize for CONSISTENCY, not accuracy. https://docs.advantagekit.org/theory/high-frequency-odometry/

Pay for CANivore + Phoenix Pro timesync when running all-CTRE. With timesync, every device samples and publishes on the same tick with a device-side timestamp, giving best-possible latency compensation; CTRE measures ~15% mean and ~34% std-dev odometry improvement on top of frequency gains. https://v6.docs.ctr-electronics.com/en/latest/docs/api-reference/mechanisms/swerve/swerve-overview.html

Apply the 254-derived swerve setpoint generator, not just wheel-speed desaturation. PathPlanner's SwerveSetpointGenerator limits module acceleration by motor torque, caps module torque at wheel-carpet friction to prevent slip, limits module rotation so centripetal force stays under friction (prevents sliding in curves), and models intra-module friction (lower max accel, higher max decel). https://pathplanner.dev/pplib-swerve-setpoint-generator.html

Characterize rather than guess — and characterize wheel radius, not just kS/kV. 6328 ships an in-code feedforward routine (2 s orient, 0.1 V/s ramp, least-squares fit) and a wheel-radius routine (spin in place at 0.05 rad/s^2 to 0.25 rad/s; radius = gyroDelta * driveBaseRadius / meanWheelDelta), explicitly recommending regular recharacterization to combat tread wear and carpet compression. Tuner X's generator does NOT characterize and its shipped gains are placeholders. https://docs.advantagekit.org/getting-started/template-projects/spark-swerve-template/

Set drive current limits from a measured slip test, not from a spec sheet. CTRE's documented procedure: put the robot against a wall on carpet, plot velocity and stator current in Tuner X, slowly increase voltage until velocity goes non-zero and stator current drops — that is the slip point (~130 A in their example), so limit below it (their swerve example: 120 A stator / 70 A supply per Kraken). https://v6.docs.ctr-electronics.com/en/stable/docs/hardware-reference/talonfx/improving-performance-with-current-limits.html

Do skid detection and feed it into odometry trust. 1690 Orbit published the canonical FRC algorithm in their 2024 software sessions; 135's Consul framework ships it alongside momentum-based setpoint calculation. Elite teams use it to know when wheel odometry is lying and to lean harder on vision. https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/writeup-on-swerve-kinematics-and-basic-skid-detection/522622 and https://oa.pennrobotics.org/135-consul-frc-programming-framework/

Separate the three heading concepts explicitly. CTRE's API distinguishes seedFieldCentric() / seedFieldCentric(Rotation2d) (driver perspective), resetRotation(Rotation2d) (absolute blue-alliance-perspective heading), and setOperatorPerspectiveForward(Rotation2d) (called periodically, 0 deg on blue and 180 deg on red). Pose origin is ALWAYS blue; only the driver's forward flips. https://v6.docs.ctr-electronics.com/en/latest/docs/api-reference/mechanisms/swerve/using-swerve-api.html

Use a ProfiledPIDController for heading lock rather than a plain P controller, with continuous input enabled. 6328's joystickDriveAtAngle uses KP=5.0, KD=0.4, max velocity 8.0 rad/s, max accel 20.0 rad/s^2, enableContinuousInput(-pi, pi). WPILib's HolonomicDriveController uses the same pattern: two PID controllers for x/y and one PROFILED controller for heading, because heading dynamics are decoupled from translation. https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Mechanical-Advantage/AdvantageKit/main/template_projects/sources/talonfx_swerve/src/main/java/frc/robot/commands/DriveCommands.java

Feed per-module wheel force feedforwards from the path planner into the drivetrain. Both PathPlanner (DriveFeedforwards) and Choreo emit them; CTRE's ApplyFieldSpeeds/ApplyRobotSpeeds accept them via withWheelForceFeedforwardsX/Y in newtons (WPILib convention, X forward). CTRE's own docs say its new-for-2026 WheelForceCalculator should be used only when your planner does NOT provide them. https://v6.docs.ctr-electronics.com/en/latest/docs/api-reference/mechanisms/swerve/swerve-requests.html

Simulate with a real physics engine, not an ideal model. CTRE's swerve sim explicitly assumes no scrub and no wheel slip with constant drive inertia. Top teams use maple-sim (dyn4j rigid-body, collisions, game pieces, 2026 REBUILT field) so simulated autos transfer to the field. 135's Consul does the same with dyn4j directly, and tunes sim constants by matching simulated to real acceleration. https://shenzhen-robotics-alliance.github.io/maple-sim/swerve-simulation-overview/

Build for log replay from day one. AdvantageKit's IO layer + @AutoLog IOInputs makes logs the ground truth so a fix can be validated against a real match without re-running the robot; 135's Consul adopted the same three-layer split (IO = zero business logic, IOInputs = timestamped @AutoLog record, Subsystem = vendor-agnostic logic). Elite teams also swap PathPlanner's pathfinder for LocalADStarAK so pathfinding itself is deterministic under replay. https://docs.advantagekit.org/getting-started/template-projects/talonfx-swerve-template/

Tune steer with a very high kP and rely on feedback, not feedforward. Tuner X ships steer Slot0 kP=100, kD=0.5, kS=0.1, kV=1.91; 6328 notes that brushless motors make swerve turning exceptionally easy to control and that a well-tuned feedback-only controller gives nearly perfect tracking. https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/frc-6328-mechanical-advantage-2026-build-thread/509595
pitfalls: WPILib 2026 SILENTLY changed SwerveModuleState optimization semantics. `optimize(Rotation2d)` and `cosineScale(Rotation2d)` are now void MUTATING INSTANCE methods; the static `SwerveModuleState optimize(SwerveModuleState, Rotation2d)` is deprecated. Code copied from 2023/2024 tutorials that does `state = SwerveModuleState.optimize(state, angle)` still compiles but is on a deprecated path, and code that half-migrates to `state.optimize(angle)` while still assigning the (void) return will not compile — teams then 'fix' it by deleting the call and lose optimization entirely, producing modules that take the long way around. https://github.wpilib.org/allwpilib/docs/release/java/edu/wpi/first/math/kinematics/SwerveModuleState.html

Forgetting ChassisSpeeds.discretize() causes the robot to arc sideways while translating and rotating simultaneously. It is never applied automatically by SwerveDriveKinematics. The mirror-image bug is DOUBLE discretization: PathPlanner's SwerveSetpointGenerator discretizes internally and its docs explicitly warn 'do not discretize speeds before or after using the setpoint generator.' https://pathplanner.dev/pplib-swerve-setpoint-generator.html

The alliance-flip trap. Pose origin is always blue; only the driver's 'forward' flips. Teams conflate 'zero the gyro' (operator perspective) with resetting the pose (absolute, blue-origin), which produces a robot that drives correctly in the shop and inverted on the red alliance, or an auto that starts from a mirrored pose. CTRE's three-method split (seedFieldCentric / resetRotation / setOperatorPerspectiveForward) exists precisely because of this. https://v6.docs.ctr-electronics.com/en/latest/docs/api-reference/mechanisms/swerve/using-swerve-api.html

WPILib 2027 is a hard break and Rootstock's API surface must be designed for it NOW: `edu.wpi.first` -> `org.wpilib` and `frc::` -> `wpi::`; `ChassisSpeeds` renamed to `ChassisVelocities`; swerve and differential kinematics made IMMUTABLE; new `ChassisAccelerations` plus forward/inverse kinematics for accelerations; `RamseteCommand`, `SwerveControllerCommand` and `MecanumControllerCommand` REMOVED; Commands v3 introduced alongside v2 and `Command.schedule()` deprecated in v2; Java 25 / C++23; NetworkTables v3 removed; Shuffleboard, SmartDashboard, PathWeaver and RobotBuilder removed; roboRIO replaced by Systemcore (multiple CAN buses, Smart IO, onboard IMU); relays, analog outputs, SPI, ADIS16448/16470, ADXL345, ADXRS450, servos and Jaguar removed. https://docs.wpilib.org/en/latest/docs/yearly-overview/yearly-changelog.html

Phoenix 6 is breaking too. In the 2027 dev line (26.50.0-alpha-1) `SwerveRequest.ApplyFieldSpeeds`/`ApplyRobotSpeeds` are renamed `ApplyFieldVelocity`/`ApplyRobotVelocity` (tracking WPILib's ChassisSpeeds->ChassisVelocities rename), and `new <Device>(int id, String canbus)` constructors are already deprecated in 26.x and REMOVED in 2027 in favor of `new <Device>(int id, CANBus canbus)`. Any Rootstock code that names those request classes must be behind an adapter. https://api.ctr-electronics.com/phoenix6/latest/java/com/ctre/phoenix6/swerve/package-summary.html and https://v6.docs.ctr-electronics.com/en/latest/docs/yearly-changes/yearly-changelog.html

Tuner X generates the project but does NOT characterize it. The shipped TunerConstants gains (drive kP=0.1, kS=0, kV=0.124; steer kP=100, kD=0.5, kS=0.1, kV=1.91) and slipCurrent=120 A are placeholders for a reference robot. Teams that never touch them get sluggish drive response and a slip current that is wrong for their weight and tread. https://v6.docs.ctr-electronics.com/en/latest/docs/api-reference/mechanisms/swerve/swerve-builder-api.html

CTRE swerve simulation assumes no scrub, no wheel slip, and constant drive motor inertia — autos tuned only in CTRE sim will not transfer. It also models azimuth inertia and control lag, so modules lag their targets; CTRE recommends driving updateSimState from a 4 ms Notifier instead of the 20 ms robot loop to get realistic PID behavior. https://v6.docs.ctr-electronics.com/en/latest/docs/api-reference/mechanisms/swerve/swerve-simulation.html

YAGSL's documented failure modes recur every season on Chief Delphi: robot freezing repeatedly while driving after a library update; module angles losing alignment under semi-aggressive driving with modules driving in reverse; turn motors spinning endlessly with no command (wrong steer inversion, or drive/steer CAN IDs swapped); odometry arcing during rotation when AprilTags are visible. YAGSL's own docs also tell all-CTRE teams to use Tuner X instead. https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/yagsl-swerve-modules-losing-alignment-when-driving/496307 and https://docs.yagsl.com/

Absolute encoder offsets and magnet mounting are the top hardware-adjacent software bug. If modules do not point straight on boot or after a straight command, offsets are wrong; a slightly-off offset drags a module and can draw penalties. Loose/unglued magnets drift the offset mid-competition. A library must ship a re-zeroing routine and a boot-time sanity check, not just a JSON field. https://docs.yagsl.com/configuring-yagsl/configuration/swerve-module-configuration

SwerveSetpointGenerator and PathPlanner's RobotConfig need massKG, MOI and wheelCOF. Nobody measures MOI; the entire community copies 74.088 kg / 6.883 kg*m^2 / 1.2 COF from the 6328 template. Wrong MOI makes slip limiting either useless (too permissive) or crippling (too conservative). https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Mechanical-Advantage/AdvantageKit/main/template_projects/sources/spark_swerve/src/main/java/frc/robot/subsystems/drive/DriveConstants.java

AdvantageKit templates are copy-and-own, not a dependency. There is no upgrade path — the 2026 templates contain 'many small changes and optimizations' versus 2025 that a team on last year's copy will never receive. A Rootstock that wraps the template inherits this; a Rootstock that adapts a team's existing Drive class does not. https://docs.advantagekit.org/whats-new/

Slew rate limiting is a traction band-aid, not a driver-feel feature. REV REMOVED the slew rate limiter from the MAXSwerve template because it is no longer needed with MAXSwerve 2.0 wheels. Shipping it on by default masks a tuning or traction problem and adds latency the driver feels. https://github.com/REVrobotics/MAXSwerve-Java-Template/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md

Module order must be identical everywhere. SwerveDriveKinematics, SwerveDriveOdometry and PathPlanner's output all assume a consistent ordering (WPILib docs: 'it is important that the order in which you pass the SwerveModulePosition objects is the same as the order in which you created the kinematics object'; PathPlanner's swerve output is FL, FR, BL, BR). A library that accepts modules as an unordered map will produce subtly wrong kinematics. https://docs.wpilib.org/en/stable/docs/software/kinematics-and-odometry/swerve-drive-odometry.html

RamseteController is deprecated for removal (since 2025) — a rookie team following an old tank tutorial in 2026 is writing code that will not compile in 2027. LTVUnicycleController is the drop-in replacement, but note its guardrails: default tolerances x=0.0625 m, y=0.125 m, heading=2 rad, default maxVelocity 9 m/s, and it throws IllegalArgumentException if maxVelocity <=0 or >=15 m/s. https://github.wpilib.org/allwpilib/docs/release/java/edu/wpi/first/math/controller/LTVUnicycleController.html

Phoenix 6 26.1.0 changed a silent default: drive motor RotorToSensorRatio and SensorToMechanismRatio and steer motor SensorToMechanismRatio are now overridden to 1.0 so odometry and control behave as expected. Teams carrying over 2025 configs that set these themselves may see doubled/halved distances. https://api.ctr-electronics.com/changelog

YAGSL odometry runs at the 20 ms loop rate rather than on a high-frequency thread, and closed-loop PID on the controller is only available for SparkMAX and TalonFX. A team on YAGSL with mixed/PWM hardware is giving up the single biggest auto-consistency lever without being told. https://docs.yagsl.com/overview/our-features

source: FRC Vision (Limelight / PhotonVision / custom) — research dossier for Rootstock, August 2026
summary: As of Aug 2026 the FRC vision stack has consolidated around two vendor products (Limelight OS 2026.1 with LimelightHelpers/LimelightLib, and PhotonVision 2026.3.4 with photonlib) plus a small but influential tier of homebrew coprocessor pipelines (6328's Northstar, Team 190's GompeiVision, 1701's CubVision) that publish raw double arrays over NT4. Both vendors now converge on the same conceptual output — a field-relative Pose3d with a capture-time timestamp, a tag count, an average tag distance, and an ambiguity — but expose it through completely incompatible APIs (Limelight: flat `botpose_orb_wpiblue` double[] on NetworkTables, gyro-fed MegaTag2, camera transform configured in the web UI; PhotonVision: `PhotonCamera.getAllUnreadResults()` returning `PhotonPipelineResult` with `multitagResult`, camera transform configured in robot code). PhotonVision 2026 deprecated the entire `PoseStrategy` enum + `PhotonPoseEstimator.update()` in favor of explicit `estimateCoprocMultiTagPose(result)` / `estimateLowestAmbiguityPose(result)` / `estimatePnpDistanceTrigSolvePose(result)` / `estimateConstrainedSolvepnpPose(...)` methods — a breaking-ish change most 2025 tutorials have not caught up with. The 2026 REBUILT field ships two layouts (`AprilTagFields.k2026RebuiltWelded`, `k2026RebuiltAndymark`) and mismatching them between coprocessor and robot code is still the single most common silent pose-estimation bug. The de-facto reference integration is the AdvantageKit vision template's `VisionIO`/`PoseObservation` abstraction, which already unifies Limelight MegaTag1, MegaTag2 and PhotonVision behind one record — Rootstock should adopt that shape, generalize it to custom sources and object detection, and add the things it lacks (a pluggable filter chain with reject reasons, a pluggable std-dev model, sim wiring for Limelight, a tag-layout override loader for WPIcal output, and vision-driven action commands). The big 2027 signal: WPILib 2027 renames all Java packages from `edu.wpi.first.*` to `org.wpilib.*`, drops NT3, and moves to Systemcore/Java 25 — AdvantageKit's main-branch templates are already written against `org.wpilib.*`, so Rootstock must keep vendor-facing code behind a thin seam or plan a mechanical rename.

landscape.tool: Limelight OS 2026 (LL4 / LL3G / LL3A / LL3 / LL2+)
landscape.doesWell: Zero-code AprilTag localization. MegaTag2 (`botpose_orb_wpiblue`) is ambiguity-free at any distance given a known yaw, and is the single best out-of-box localizer for a small team. LL4 has an internal IMU with 5 fusion modes (0 EXTERNAL_ONLY, 1 EXTERNAL_SEED, 2 INTERNAL_ONLY, 3 INTERNAL_MT1_ASSIST, 4 INTERNAL_EXTERNAL_ASSIST — mode 4 recommended). 2026.1 adds `tdist` (3D distance to target/POI), map POI offsets so all six Hub tags aim at Hub center, Hailo-8L default detector model, Hailo-accelerated AprilTags (up to 50% faster at 1x downscale), zero-shot classification, learning-based OCR (`rawocr`), neural detector clustering, WebRTC/H.264 streaming (46-91% bandwidth reduction). 2026.0 adds Rewind (.rwnd synchronized video+targeting+config capture, LL4 only), rebuilt ChArUco calibration workflow (~3x more detected corners), middle-of-exposure capture timestamps, free H100-backed neural net trainer at tools.limelightvision.io, skewed/perspective crop windows, NaN guards on all NT/JSON outputs. Sensors: LL4 and LL3G = OV9281 mono global shutter, 120FPS @ 1280x800 (LL3G also 240fps @ 640x480), FOV H:82° V:56.2°; LL3A/LL3 = OV5647 color rolling shutter.
landscape.gaps: Closed source. Camera-to-robot transform lives in the web UI / `camerapose_robotspace_set`, not in robot code — so it is invisible to sim and to AdvantageKit replay unless you mirror it. No first-party WPILib simulation path at all. MegaTag2 hard-requires `SetRobotOrientation` every frame or you get garbage. Pipeline switching is not instantaneous and there is no documented settle API — you must gate on `getCurrentPipelineIndex`/`getpipe` matching your request. LL4 dropped PoE (5V-26V buck-boost, 12W max), so wiring differs from LL3. `botpose` array packing is positional and undocumented in the LimelightHelpers Javadoc — you must read source. Latency accounting: the total latency is index 6 of the botpose array in ms, and `tl`+`cl` are separate keys; getting this wrong shifts your pose by 50-100ms of robot motion.

landscape.doesWell: This is the de-facto reference vendor-agnostic vision layer and Rootstock should treat it as the baseline to beat. It defines `VisionIO` with `@AutoLog VisionIOInputs { boolean connected; TargetObservation latestTargetObservation; PoseObservation[] poseObservations; int[] tagIds; }`, `record TargetObservation(Rotation2d tx, Rotation2d ty)`, `record PoseObservation(double timestamp, Pose3d pose, double ambiguity, int tagCount, double averageTagDistance, PoseObservationType type)`, `enum PoseObservationType { MEGATAG_1, MEGATAG_2, PHOTONVISION }`, and `@FunctionalInterface VisionConsumer { void accept(Pose2d, double timestampSeconds, Matrix<N3,N1> stdDevs); }`. Implementations: `VisionIOLimelight(String name, Supplier<Rotation2d> rotationSupplier)`, `VisionIOPhotonVision(String name, Transform3d robotToCamera)`, `VisionIOPhotonVisionSim(String name, Transform3d, Supplier<Pose2d>)`. Verbatim rejection filter: reject if `tagCount==0`, or `tagCount==1 && ambiguity>maxAmbiguity(0.3)`, or `abs(pose.getZ())>maxZError(0.75)`, or pose outside `[0, layout.getFieldLength()] x [0, layout.getFieldWidth()]`. Verbatim std-dev model: `stdDevFactor = pow(averageTagDistance,2)/tagCount; linear = 0.02*factor; angular = 0.06*factor;` then `*= 0.5` linear and `*= POSITIVE_INFINITY` angular for MEGATAG_2, then `*= cameraStdDevFactors[i]`. Logs `TagPoses`, `RobotPoses`, `RobotPosesAccepted`, `RobotPosesRejected` per camera plus a `Vision/Summary` table. Uses FPGA timestamps throughout so estimates go straight into a WPILib pose estimator with no CTRE `Utils.fpgaToCurrentTime()` conversion.
landscape.gaps: No object-detection path. No custom/NT-raw source. Rejection is a hardcoded boolean expression, not a pluggable chain, and rejected poses lose their reason. Std-dev model is hardcoded. Limelight has no sim implementation. No drive-to-pose / aim commands. No tag-layout override loading (WPIcal output). Single global `aprilTagLayout` static, so you cannot A/B a calibrated layout at runtime. `VisionIOLimelight` calls `NetworkTableInstance.getDefault().flush()` every loop (their own comment: "Increases network traffic but recommended by Limelight").

landscape.doesWell: Two-stage tool. Stage 1: camera intrinsics from a ChArUco video (5x5 ArUco dictionary), solvable with OpenCV or mrcal backends (mrcal recommended), producing `cameracalibration.json`. Stage 2: field calibration — film field tags from many angles with the same camera, supply an ideal field-map JSON as reference, designate one 'pinned' tag as ground truth, and it optimizes all other tag poses relative to it. Outputs both a WPILib-format `.json` layout and a Limelight `.fmap`. Field-agnostic; supports custom layouts and combining multiple partial field calibrations. Includes a visualizer showing per-tag meter/degree deltas vs the ideal layout.
landscape.gaps: Docs are explicit: 'not a silver bullet' — it only corrects minor placement error and only pays off for teams that already do everything else right. Tags must start approximately correct. Requires video capture discipline (Linux users must transcode to MJPEG .avi). No official guidance on doing this at a competition event in a 20-minute window, and no automated pipeline to push the result to both robot code and coprocessors.

landscape.tool: Custom coprocessor pipelines: Northstar (6328), GompeiVision (Team 190), CubVision (1701)
landscape.doesWell: Northstar is the reference homebrew design: Python + OpenCV ArUco on Orange Pi 5, one process per camera, publishing raw `double[]` frames over NT4 with `PubSubOption.keepDuplicates(true), sendAll(true), pollStorage(5), periodic(0.01)` so the RIO gets *every* frame with a real NT server timestamp, not a 50Hz snapshot. Config is pushed *down* from robot code over NT (`<device>/config/camera_id, camera_resolution_width/height, camera_auto_exposure, camera_exposure, camera_gain, camera_denoise, camera_balance_red/blue, fiducial_size_m, tag_layout, throttle_fps, is_recording, event_name, match_type, match_number, timestamp`) so all vision config is version-controlled in the robot repo. Outputs on `<device>/output/observations` (double[]), `objdetect_observations` (double[]), `fps_apriltags`, `fps_objdetect` (int). Supports on-camera match recording gated on FMS attachment, and per-camera `stdDevFactor` + tunable pitch fudge factors.
landscape.gaps: No web UI, no calibration UI, no packaging — you build and flash your own image. Wire format is positional and self-invented (see integrationShape), so nothing else can read it. Requires a Python + OpenCV toolchain competency most small teams don't have. Not a product: 6328 publish it, they don't support it.
landscape.version2026: RobotCode2026Public ('Darwin'), `northstar/` directory, MIT license
landscape.integrationShape:
Northstar 2026 wire format, decoded from `Vision.java` + `vision_types.py`:
- `observations` double[]: `[0]=poseCount (0,1,2)`. If 1 (multi-tag): `[1]=error0, [2..4]=x,y,z, [5..8]=quaternion(w,x,y,z)`, tag blocks start at index 9. If 2 (single tag, both PnP solutions): `[1]=error0, [2..8]=pose0`, `[9]=error1, [10..16]=pose1`, tag blocks start at index 17. Tag blocks are stride 10: `tag_id, 8 corner angles (tx,ty x4), distance`. Poses are CAMERA poses in field space; robot pose = `cameraPose.transformBy(robotToCamera.inverse())`.
- `objdetect_observations` double[] (read as float[]): stride 10 per detection: `class_id, confidence, then 4 (tx,ty) corner-angle pairs`. In 2026 class 0 = FUEL, class 1 = ROBOT.
Rootstock should adopt a *versioned, struct-serialized* successor of this (see capabilities) rather than a positional double array, but must ship a `NorthstarSchema` decoder so teams can drop in existing Northstar/CubVision/GompeiVision coprocessors unchanged.

landscape.doesWell: `AutoBuilder.pathfindToPose(Pose2d targetPose, PathConstraints constraints, double goalEndVelocity)` produces an on-the-fly obstacle-avoiding command to any pose — the natural back half of 'see tag -> drive to scoring pose'. capabilities.capability: `VisionFrame` — one immutable vendor-neutral observation record that every source produces
capabilities.whyItMatters: A small team cannot afford to rewrite its pose-estimation logic when it swaps a Limelight for a PhotonVision Orange Pi mid-season, or when a camera dies at an event and the only spare is a different brand. One record type means the filter chain, the std-dev model, the logging, the replay and the dashboard are written once and work for all three vendors plus sim. This is the single highest-leverage thing in the whole domain.
capabilities.prerequisites: None. Do this first; everything else depends on it.

capabilities.capability: `VisionCameraIO` + `@AutoLog` inputs, with Limelight / PhotonVision / Custom-NT / Sim implementations
capabilities.whyItMatters: AdvantageKit-style IO layers are what make a small team's vision system debuggable: every frame that entered the robot is in the log, so a bad pose at a competition can be replayed on a laptop that night and the fix verified without the field. The user already runs AdvantageKit, so this must be `@AutoLog`-native, not bolted on. Crucially it must also work *without* AdvantageKit for teams that don't use it.
capabilities.prerequisites: VisionFrame; a `VisionFrameStruct` implementing `edu.wpi.first.util.struct.Struct<VisionFrame>` so AdvantageKit can log frames without flattening to parallel arrays.

capabilities.capability: Pluggable filter chain with named reject reasons, replacing the hardcoded boolean
capabilities.whyItMatters: The AdvantageKit template's filter is one boolean expression; when a small team's robot teleports at an event they get no signal about *why*. A filter chain that records a `RejectReason` per frame, logs a per-reason counter, and surfaces a dashboard histogram converts 'vision is broken' into 'camera 2 rejected 340 frames for GYRO_DISAGREEMENT in match 14' — which a student can act on. This is the difference between a small team debugging in the pit and a small team giving up on vision.
capabilities.prerequisites: VisionFrame; access to `SwerveDrivePoseEstimator.sampleAt(double)` for gyro-disagreement and pose-jump checks.

capabilities.capability: Pluggable standard-deviation model with the three known-good presets built in
capabilities.whyItMatters: Std-dev tuning is where teams' vision quietly fails — the estimator either ignores vision or snaps to it. Shipping the two field-proven models verbatim (AdvantageKit's `d²/n` and 6328's `d²/n²`) with the MegaTag2 angular=∞ rule baked in gives a small team elite-tier behavior on day one, and the interface lets them evolve.
capabilities.prerequisites: VisionFrame

capabilities.capability: `RootstockVision` builder — the three-lines-of-config front door
capabilities.whyItMatters: This is the whole thesis. A small team should get multi-camera, multi-vendor, filtered, std-dev-scaled, fully-logged, sim-capable pose estimation from a dozen lines in RobotContainer, and should be able to add a fourth camera of a different brand by adding one line. Every capability above is plumbing; this is the product.
capabilities.prerequisites: VisionCameraIO, VisionFilter, StdDevModel

capabilities.capability: Transparent simulation for ALL sources, including Limelight, on one switch
capabilities.whyItMatters: Limelight has no simulation story at all — which means a Limelight team cannot test autos or alignment without a robot and a field, the two things a small team has least of. Wrapping every source in PhotonVision's `VisionSystemSim` (including Limelight, by simulating it as a PhotonCamera and re-encoding the output into the Limelight-shaped `VisionFrame`) is genuinely novel and very high value.
capabilities.prerequisites: photonlib on the classpath (already a dependency); VisionCameraIO. Note limitation: sim will not reproduce MegaTag2's gyro-fused ambiguity resolution, so sim is optimistic — document it.

capabilities.capability: A versioned struct-serialized wire schema for custom coprocessors + a matching Python publisher package
capabilities.whyItMatters: Every homebrew vision system in FRC reinvents a positional double array (Northstar, CubVision, GompeiVision all differ) and every one of them gets timestamping subtly wrong. WPILib 2026 has first-class struct serialization on NetworkTables (`StructPublisher`/`StructArrayPublisher`, `Struct<T>` with 'struct:' type strings) — nobody has used it to define a *standard* FRC vision wire format. Doing so is the genuine gap in this domain and is cheap to build.
capabilities.prerequisites: VisionFrame + a hand-written `Struct<VisionFrame>` implementation (variable-length target lists need a fixed max-targets cap or a nested struct-array topic). Publish the schema string and version it.

capabilities.capability: Field-layout resolution + live tag-residual health monitoring
capabilities.whyItMatters: Welded-vs-AndyMark layout mismatch is the #1 silent pose bug and it is invisible without instrumentation. And WPIcal output does a team no good if deploying it means hand-editing three places (robot code, PhotonVision UI, Limelight .fmap). Making the layout a single resolved artifact with a visible per-tag residual turns a mystery into a number.
capabilities.prerequisites: VisionFrame with `bestCameraToTarget` populated (Limelight: `getRawFiducials()`/`targetpose_cameraspace`; PhotonVision: `target.bestCameraToTarget`).

capabilities.capability: Vision-driven action commands: align-to-pose, aim-at-point, auto-intake, shoot-on-the-fly solver
capabilities.whyItMatters: This is the payoff a small team actually sees on the field. Elite teams structure alignment as a two-phase (pathfind then terminal-PID) command with an explicit freshness gate and a tag-id filter; small teams write a `while(tx > 1) turn()` loop that oscillates. Shipping these as composable commands, with the vision freshness/rejection gating already wired, is a direct competitive transfer.
capabilities.prerequisites: RootstockVision, a Drive interface, PathPlannerLib (optional dependency — degrade to pure terminal control if absent). The shot solver is a fixed-point iteration on time-of-flight; 3-5 iterations converge in practice. Game-specific lookup tables must be team-supplied — Rootstock supplies the solver and the tuning UI, not the numbers.

capabilities.capability: Typed SnapScript / custom-payload channel (`llrobot` <-> `llpython`)
capabilities.whyItMatters: The Limelight Python pipeline is the only way a small team gets custom CV without buying and maintaining a second coprocessor, and today the robot<->script contract is two untyped double arrays that drift silently. A declared codec makes homebrew CV safe for a team with one programmer.
capabilities.prerequisites: LimelightHelpers vendored

capabilities.capability: Pipeline switching with settle detection
capabilities.whyItMatters: Switching a Limelight pipeline is not instantaneous and there is no documented completion signal; teams read stale targeting data from the previous pipeline for several frames and act on it. A command that switches and waits for `getpipe` to match AND for a fresh heartbeat is a five-line fix for a bug that costs matches.
capabilities.prerequisites: VisionCameraIO

capabilities.capability: Calibration health checker + a 'why is my vision bad' diagnostic page
capabilities.whyItMatters: The user explicitly wants software that teaches students. The vision analogue of a PID tuner is a diagnostic that says: your calibration reprojection error is 1.8px (should be <1.0), your computed FOV is 63° but your datasheet says 82° (recalibrate), camera 2's frames are arriving 180ms late (check network), tag 7's residual is 9cm (field or layout problem), 41% of camera 1's frames were rejected for HIGH_AMBIGUITY (you are relying on single tags at range).
capabilities.prerequisites: RootstockVision, TagResidualMonitor, filter chain reject counters

eliteTeamPractices: Read EVERY camera frame, not the latest one. 6328 subscribe with `PubSubOption.keepDuplicates(true), sendAll(true), pollStorage(5), periodic(0.01)` and drain with `readQueue()`; PhotonVision deprecated `getLatestResult()` in favor of `getAllUnreadResults()` for exactly this reason ('can miss results, or provide duplicate ones'). A 120fps camera on a 50Hz loop loses 60% of its data otherwise. Sources: https://github.com/Mechanical-Advantage/RobotCode2026Public/blob/main/src/main/java/org/littletonrobotics/frc2026/subsystems/vision/VisionIONorthstar.java , https://github.com/PhotonVision/photonvision/blob/v2026.1.1/photon-lib/src/main/java/org/photonvision/PhotonCamera.java

Scale vision standard deviations by distance² and by tag count. AdvantageKit template: `stdDevFactor = pow(avgTagDistance,2)/tagCount`, linear baseline 0.02 m, angular baseline 0.06 rad. 6328's 2026 Darwin code is more aggressive: `xyStdDev = 0.01 * d² / n² * cameraFactor` and `thetaStdDev = 0.03 * d² / n² * cameraFactor` — note n SQUARED, so two tags are 4x more trusted, not 2x. Sources: https://github.com/Mechanical-Advantage/AdvantageKit/blob/main/template_projects/sources/vision/src/main/java/frc/robot/subsystems/vision/Vision.java , https://github.com/Mechanical-Advantage/RobotCode2026Public/blob/main/src/main/java/org/littletonrobotics/frc2026/subsystems/vision/VisionConstants.java

Never let vision correct heading when a gyro is available. 6328 set `thetaStdDev = Double.POSITIVE_INFINITY` whenever the observation is a disambiguated single-tag solve; the AdvantageKit template sets `angularStdDevMegatag2Factor = Double.POSITIVE_INFINITY`; Limelight's own docs recommend `VecBuilder.fill(0.7, 0.7, 9999999)` for MegaTag2. Vision heading is the noisiest channel and the one you least need. Sources: https://docs.limelightvision.io/docs/docs-limelight/pipeline-apriltag/apriltag-robot-localization-megatag2 , https://github.com/Mechanical-Advantage/RobotCode2026Public/blob/main/src/main/java/org/littletonrobotics/frc2026/subsystems/vision/Vision.java

Disambiguate single-tag PnP by comparing BOTH solutions against the current gyro heading, rather than trusting the solver's ambiguity ranking. 6328 accept a single-tag frame only when `error0 < error1*0.4 || error1 < error0*0.4` (ambiguityThreshold = 0.4) and then pick whichever of the two candidate robot poses is closer in rotation to `RobotState.getRotation()`. This is strictly better than a plain ambiguity threshold. Source: https://github.com/Mechanical-Advantage/RobotCode2026Public/blob/main/src/main/java/org/littletonrobotics/frc2026/subsystems/vision/Vision.java

Reject on physics, not just on statistics: field bounds with a margin (6328 use fieldBorderMargin = 0.5 m), Z bounds (6328 use zMin = -0.5, zMax = 1.0 m; AdvantageKit uses |z| < 0.75), and angular rate (Limelight's own MegaTag2 sample rejects when `|gyro.getRate()| > 360` deg/s). A pose that puts the robot 40cm off the floor is wrong regardless of its reported ambiguity. Sources: https://github.com/Mechanical-Advantage/RobotCode2026Public/blob/main/src/main/java/org/littletonrobotics/frc2026/subsystems/vision/VisionConstants.java , https://docs.limelightvision.io/docs/docs-limelight/pipeline-apriltag/apriltag-robot-localization-megatag2

Ignore vision for the first seconds of autonomous. 6328 carry `autoIgnoreTimeSecs = 2.0` — during the initial burst of motion the odometry is trustworthy and vision is at its worst (motion blur, tags at extreme angle), and a bad correction in the first second wrecks the whole auto. Source: https://github.com/Mechanical-Advantage/RobotCode2026Public/blob/main/src/main/java/org/littletonrobotics/frc2026/subsystems/vision/VisionConstants.java

Log accepted AND rejected poses separately, every loop. The AdvantageKit template logs `RobotPoses`, `RobotPosesAccepted`, `RobotPosesRejected` and `TagPoses` per camera plus a Summary table; the entire debugging workflow (drive teleop, watch in AdvantageScope, tune the rejection thresholds) depends on rejected poses being visible rather than dropped. Source: https://docs.advantagekit.org/getting-started/template-projects/vision-template/

Push camera configuration DOWN from robot code, don't configure it in a web UI. 6328's Northstar takes camera id, resolution, exposure, gain, denoise, white balance, fiducial size, tag layout and throttle over NT `config/` topics — so every vision parameter is in git and identical across four coprocessors. Limelight's web-UI-only camera transform is the opposite pattern and is why Limelight teams cannot simulate or replay. Source: https://github.com/Mechanical-Advantage/RobotCode2026Public/blob/main/src/main/java/org/littletonrobotics/frc2026/subsystems/vision/VisionIONorthstar.java

Model the camera transform as a function of time, not a constant, when a camera is on a moving mechanism. 6328's `CameraConfig.poseFunction` is `Function<Double timestamp, Optional<Pose3d>>` — it returns empty when the mechanism angle at that timestamp is unknown, which correctly drops the frame instead of using a wrong transform. Also note their per-camera `cameraPitchFudgeDegrees` LoggedTunableNumbers (one camera at -4.5°): mounting is never as-CADded. Source: https://github.com/Mechanical-Advantage/RobotCode2026Public/blob/main/src/main/java/org/littletonrobotics/frc2026/subsystems/vision/VisionConstants.java

Feed the gyro to the camera every single loop and flush NT immediately. MegaTag2 is worthless without it. The AdvantageKit Limelight IO writes `robot_orientation_set` then calls `NetworkTableInstance.getDefault().flush()` with the comment 'Increases network traffic but recommended by Limelight'. On LL4, prefer IMU mode 4 (INTERNAL_EXTERNAL_ASSIST) so the internal IMU carries you between external updates. Sources: https://github.com/Mechanical-Advantage/AdvantageKit/blob/main/template_projects/sources/vision/src/main/java/frc/robot/subsystems/vision/VisionIOLimelight.java , https://docs.limelightvision.io/docs/docs-limelight/pipeline-apriltag/apriltag-robot-localization-megatag2

Calibrate at the exact resolution you will run, with a ChArUco board, and check the numbers. PhotonVision docs: calibration is specific to each physical camera AND each resolution; mean reprojection error should be under ~1 px; computed FOV should match the datasheet within ±10°; take at least 12 images at varying distances and up to 45° tilts; mount the board rigidly and flat, never handheld; print at 100% and measure the printed markers with calipers. Prefer the mrcal backend over OpenCV. Source: https://docs.photonvision.org/en/latest/docs/calibration/calibration.html

Calibrate the FIELD, not just the camera, once everything else is right. WPIcal measures real tag positions relative to a pinned reference tag and emits both a WPILib layout JSON and a Limelight .fmap. WPILib is explicit that this yields limited benefit and only for teams that have already done everything else correctly — so it is the last optimization, not the first. Source: https://docs.wpilib.org/en/stable/docs/software/wpilib-tools/wpical/index.html

Run object detection as tx/ty corner observations, not as poses. 6328's 2026 object pipeline publishes, per detection, `class_id, confidence, and the four corner (tx,ty) angle pairs` — the robot code then projects onto the ground plane using the known camera transform. This is far more robust than trusting a coprocessor's 3D estimate of a sphere. They also explicitly track opposing ROBOTS as class 1 alongside game pieces as class 0. Source: https://github.com/Mechanical-Advantage/RobotCode2026Public/blob/main/src/main/java/org/littletonrobotics/frc2026/subsystems/vision/Vision.java

Alert loudly when a camera goes quiet. Both 6328's Vision subsystem (a 1.5 s disconnect timer plus a separate NT-connection check, distinguishing 'connected to NT but not publishing frames' from 'disconnected from NT') and the AdvantageKit template raise WPILib `Alert`s. A silently dead camera degrades pose estimation invisibly. Source: https://github.com/Mechanical-Advantage/RobotCode2026Public/blob/main/src/main/java/org/littletonrobotics/frc2026/subsystems/vision/Vision.java

Record match video on the camera, gated on FMS attachment. 6328 debounce `DriverStation.isFMSAttached()` by 3 s and push `is_recording` to every Northstar; Limelight OS 2026 ships Rewind on LL4 (always-buffering, zero disk cost until saved, .rwnd bundles synchronized video + targeting + hardware + config, ~500µs-1ms latency penalty). Post-match video of what the camera actually saw is how elite teams resolve 'the robot went the wrong way'. Sources: https://github.com/Mechanical-Advantage/RobotCode2026Public/blob/main/src/main/java/org/littletonrobotics/frc2026/subsystems/vision/Vision.java , https://docs.limelightvision.io/docs/docs-limelight/software-change-log

Throttle vision when you need CPU elsewhere. 6328 push `throttle_fps` to every camera based on a global `Robot.shouldThrottle()`; Limelight exposes `throttle_set` (skip N frames between processed frames, also for thermal control) and `fiducial_downscale_set`. Source: https://docs.limelightvision.io/docs/docs-limelight/apis/complete-networktables-api

Use `PoseEstimator.sampleAt(double timestamp)` rather than the current pose when you need the robot pose that corresponds to a vision frame or a shot. It is the only correct way to compare a vision heading against the gyro heading at capture time, and the only correct way to aim at a latency-compensated target. Source: https://github.wpilib.org/allwpilib/docs/release/java/edu/wpi/first/math/estimator/SwerveDrivePoseEstimator.html

For shoot-on-the-fly, move the target, not the robot: subtract `v_robot * timeOfFlight` from the goal position and re-solve, iterating because time-of-flight depends on the corrected range. Requires a turret or a swerve that can rotate independently of translation. Expect the flywheel/hood setpoints to be continuously moving, so feedforward-dominant control matters more than tight PID. Source: https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/advice-on-shooting-while-moving/405472
pitfalls: WELDED vs ANDYMARK layout mismatch. `AprilTagFields.k2026RebuiltWelded` and `k2026RebuiltAndymark` are different fields. PhotonVision ships with the WELDED layout by default; if your robot code loads AndyMark (or vice versa) you get a plausible-looking pose that is wrong by inches to feet, with no error. Verify on BOTH the coprocessor and the roboRIO. https://docs.photonvision.org/en/latest/docs/apriltag-pipelines/multitag.html

MegaTag2 with no gyro feed = garbage. `botpose_orb_wpiblue` is only valid if `robot_orientation_set` / `SetRobotOrientation(name, yaw, 0,0,0,0,0)` is written every frame, blue-origin, CCW-positive, 0° facing the red wall. Writing it once at init produces a pose that looks fine at startup and drifts silently. https://docs.limelightvision.io/docs/docs-limelight/pipeline-apriltag/apriltag-robot-localization-megatag2

Feeding MegaTag2 the pose estimator's own heading creates a feedback loop. Limelight's sample uses `m_poseEstimator.getEstimatedPosition().getRotation()`, but if vision is also correcting rotation you have a loop. Set angular std dev to infinity (or 9999999) whenever you use MegaTag2, so the gyro is the sole heading authority.

Limelight latency accounting. Total latency for a botpose sample is at index 6 of the array, in MILLISECONDS, and must be subtracted from the NT sample timestamp (in microseconds): `ts = sample.timestamp*1e-6 - value[6]*1e-3`. `tl` (pipeline) and `cl` (capture) are separate NT keys and are NOT the same as index 6. Getting this wrong at 4 m/s shifts your pose by ~20-40 cm. Verified in AdvantageKit `VisionIOLimelight`.
`getBotPoseEstimate_*()` returns only the newest sample. On a 120fps LL4 with a 50Hz loop you throw away over half your frames. Use `readQueue()` on the raw NT topic instead.
`getLatestResults()` (LimelightHelpers) parses the entire JSON dump on the roboRIO. Calling it every loop is a well-known loop-overrun source. Use typed getters or raw NT.

PhotonVision 2026 deprecated the entire `PoseStrategy` path. `PhotonPoseEstimator(layout, strategy, robotToCamera)`, `setPrimaryStrategy`, `setMultiTagFallbackStrategy`, `setReferencePose`, `setLastPose` and all `update(...)` overloads are `@Deprecated(forRemoval=true, since="2026")`. Code copied from 2024/2025 tutorials compiles with warnings today and will break. Use `estimateCoprocMultiTagPose(result)` with an `estimateLowestAmbiguityPose(result)` fallback.

`estimatePnpDistanceTrigSolvePose` and `estimateConstrainedSolvepnpPose` silently do nothing useful without `addHeadingData(timestamp, heading)` being called every loop. `estimateRioMultiTagPose` and `estimateConstrainedSolvepnpPose` also require `camera.getCameraMatrix()` and `camera.getDistCoeffs()`, both `Optional` and both EMPTY if the camera is uncalibrated at the current resolution.

PhotonVision 3D mode requires calibration at the exact streaming resolution. Calibrating at 1280x800 and streaming at 640x400 gives you no 3D output (or wrong output). Recalibrate per resolution. https://docs.photonvision.org/en/latest/docs/calibration/calibration.html

`addVisionMeasurement()` silently no-ops when the timestamp is outside the internal odometry buffer (~1.5 s). A coprocessor whose clock is not NT-synced, or one that publishes wall-clock instead of NT time, produces zero vision correction and zero error messages. Always assert timestamp sanity and log the delta between now and the frame timestamp.

Do not mix time bases. WPILib pose estimators use FPGA time. CTRE Phoenix 6 swerve uses its own 'current time' and requires `Utils.fpgaToCurrentTime()` when feeding `addVisionMeasurement` on a `SwerveDrivetrain`. AdvantageKit's template deliberately uses FPGA timestamps end-to-end so no conversion is needed. Mixing the two produces a constant offset error proportional to speed.

Single-tag coplanar PnP ambiguity flipping. Limelight's own docs: 'If all keypoints are coplanar, there is still some risk of ambiguity flipping.' Their MegaTag1 sample rejects single-tag frames with `ambiguity > 0.7` or `distToCamera > 3` m. AdvantageKit uses `maxAmbiguity = 0.3`. Pick a threshold and also cross-check against gyro heading.

Pose estimation degrades when the camera is normal (perpendicular) to the tag plane — the classic PnP degenerate case. Mount cameras with deliberate yaw/pitch offset rather than staring straight at the tag; 6328 mount at ±70° yaw and 12° pitch. https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/pose-estimation-degrades-when-the-camera-is-normal-to-the-apriltag-plane/514907

Limelight camera-to-robot transform lives in the web UI, not in code. If the camera is reflashed, swapped, or a spare is installed, the transform is gone and every pose is wrong by the mount offset. Push it from robot code with `setCameraPose_RobotSpace` / `camerapose_robotspace_set` at startup, and log what you pushed.

Limelight 4 dropped PoE. It is 5V-26V buck-boost input (3.5V-35V absolute max), 12W max, via a Weidmuller port — you cannot reuse an LL3 PoE injector. https://docs.limelightvision.io/docs/docs-limelight/getting-started/limelight-4

Limelight OS 2026.0 requirement: wall-mounted tags in 2026 maps will not display correctly until LLOS 2026.0 is installed, and Hailo neural models from the 2026 trainer require LLOS 2026.0. Also, AprilTag acceleration on Hailo was temporarily DISABLED in 2026.0 and returned in 2026.1 (up to 50% faster at 1x downscale). https://docs.limelightvision.io/docs/docs-limelight/software-change-log

Pipeline switching has real latency and no completion signal. Poll `getpipe`/`getCurrentPipelineIndex` until it matches AND the heartbeat `hb` has advanced before trusting targeting data. UNVERIFIED: the exact settle time is not documented; measure it.

`snapshot` semantics changed in LLOS 2026.0 from a level to a rising-edge counter (0→1→2→3), rate-limited to 1 per 10 frames. Code that sets `snapshot=1` and leaves it will capture once and then stop.

Running OpenCV AprilTag detection on the roboRIO is a trap. WPILib's own vision guidance and every elite team put it on a coprocessor: the RIO's CPU is needed for the 20ms control loop, and tag detection at usable resolution will blow the loop time. Use the RIO only for consuming results. https://docs.wpilib.org/en/stable/docs/software/vision-processing/introduction/strategies-for-vision-programming.html

Custom-coprocessor timestamping is where homebrew systems die. You must publish MIDDLE-OF-EXPOSURE time (Limelight OS 2026.0 changed to this convention explicitly, using middle-row for rolling shutter) converted into NT server time, not camera monotonic time and not wall clock. If you cannot do this, do not build a custom pipeline.

Rolling shutter (LL3A, LL3, most cheap USB cameras) smears tags under rotation. Global shutter (OV9281 on LL4/LL3G, OV2311 on Arducam) is worth the money for anything moving. PhotonVision docs: 'Global shutter cameras are recommended in all cases.'
PhotonVision does not support Logitech cameras, built-in webcams, or virtual cameras — this bites teams who buy the cheapest USB camera on the shelf.

WPILib 2027 will break every import. `edu.wpi.first.*` becomes `org.wpilib.*`, C++ `frc::` becomes `wpi::`, NT3 is removed, `robotInit()` is removed, and the platform moves to Systemcore/Java 25. AdvantageKit's main-branch templates are ALREADY written against `org.wpilib.*`. Rootstock must keep all WPILib types behind a thin internal seam or accept a mechanical rename in Oct 2026. https://docs.wpilib.org/en/latest/docs/yearly-overview/yearly-changelog.html

AprilTagFieldLayout.setOrigin() mutates a shared object. If two subsystems hold the same layout instance and one flips the origin for red alliance, the other silently sees flipped tag poses. Treat the layout as immutable; use the wpiblue-origin convention everywhere (which is what both vendors emit since 2024).

WPIcal is not magic. WPILib's own docs: it 'is not a silver bullet of computer vision accuracy', it only corrects minor placement error, tags must start approximately correct, and it only pays off after every other localization practice is already right. Do not sell field calibration as a first step.

PathPlanner `pathfindToPose` will happily drive to a pose computed from a stale or rejected vision estimate. Always gate alignment commands on vision freshness and hand off to a terminal controller for the last ~0.5 m.

Object-detection models are game-specific and licensed. PhotonVision's shipped COCO and 2026 FUEL models are AGPLv3 (Ultralytics). PhotonVision explicitly does not support training, only conversion, and object detection is only available on specific hardware (Orange Pi 5 / Rubik Pi 3 as of 2026). Limelight's trainer is free but produces Limelight-format models tied to Hailo 8 / 8L / Coral / CPU runtimes. Do not promise portable models.

PhotonVision 2026.1.1 (the user's pinned version) is the January release; 2026.3.4 (April) is the current stable and includes the FUEL detection models, the 127-target limit raise, and the OV9281 autoexposure fix. Pin bumps matter here.

summary: As of August 2026 the FRC autonomous stack has consolidated onto two interoperable tools plus a hand-rolled tier. PathPlanner 2026.1.2 (Jan 12 2026) is a GUI-first, spline-based planner whose 2025 ground-up rewrite replaced replanning/ReplanningConfig with a torque/friction-aware trajectory generator driven by RobotConfig (mass, MOI, module offsets, wheel COF, drive motor, current limit) and emits per-module DriveFeedforwards that feed straight into Phoenix 6's SwerveRequest.ApplyRobotSpeeds.withWheelForceFeedforwardsX/Y; it uniquely owns on-the-fly pathfinding (AD*/LocalADStar over deploy/pathplanner/navgrid.json) via AutoBuilder.pathfindToPose / pathfindThenFollowPath. Choreo 2026 (v2026.0.3, Apr 6 2026) is a time-optimal numerical optimizer (TrajoptLib on Sleipnir) that produces pre-baked .traj files and, critically, ships ChoreoLib's AutoFactory/AutoRoutine/AutoTrajectory — a trigger-based composition API (atTime, atTimeBeforeEnd, atTranslation, atPose, done, doneDelayed, recentlyDone, anyDone, anyActive) that is strictly more expressive for mechanism coordination than PathPlanner's NamedCommands, and it cannot regenerate from the robot's actual starting state. The two are complementary, not competing: PathPlannerPath.fromChoreoTrajectory(name, splitIndex) lets PPLib follow Choreo output, and PathPlannerAuto now exposes the same trigger surface (event, beforeEvent, distanceFromEvent, nearFieldPositionAutoFlipped, inFieldAreaAutoFlipped, timeRange, condition) plus a mirror constructor. Elite teams do not use either library's auto files as the top-level structure: 6328's 2026 code loads Choreo Trajectory<SwerveSample> but follows it with a custom DriveTrajectory command (3 PIDs + trajectory feedforward + an omega override for shoot-on-the-move) and composes autos from question-driven AutoSelector responses; 254's 2025 auto was fully dynamic — a scoring-sequence string from a custom dashboard driving AD* pathfinding with per-phase navgrids, retry-on-failed-intake, and a 12-second "skip to starred step" budget; 1678's 2026 code uses ChoreoLib AutoFactory with factory.bind() global event markers plus an AutoModeBase wrapper adding mirroring and collision detection; 2910 uses Choreo.TrajectoryCache with a Superstructure state enum. The genuine gaps Rootstock should fill are (a) a single trigger/composition surface that works identically over PathPlanner and Choreo trajectories, (b) a superstructure request bus with graph-search transitions (254 ships an AStarSolver over superstructure states), (c) a headless auto validation harness that replays every auto variant in maple-sim and asserts a timing budget, and (d) an auto-chooser with dependent questions. WPILib 2027 is a hard break — Systemcore, Java 25, org.wpilib packages, Commands v3 coroutines, Shuffleboard/SmartDashboard/PathWeaver/RobotBuilder removed — so any Rootstock auto API must be a thin facade over the command framework, not a fork of it.

landscape.doesWell: GUI path+auto editor with waypoints, rotation targets, constraint zones, point-towards zones, and zoned/non-zoned event markers. AutoBuilder.configure(Supplier<Pose2d> poseSupplier, Consumer<Pose2d> resetPose, Supplier<ChassisSpeeds> robotRelativeSpeeds, BiConsumer<ChassisSpeeds,DriveFeedforwards> output, PathFollowingController, RobotConfig, BooleanSupplier shouldFlipPath, Subsystem... driveRequirements). Only mainstream lib with on-the-fly pathfinding: AutoBuilder.pathfindToPose(Pose2d, PathConstraints[, goalEndVelocity]), pathfindToPoseFlipped(...), pathfindThenFollowPath(PathPlannerPath, PathConstraints), backed by AD*/LocalADStar over deploy/pathplanner/navgrid.json. Regenerates trajectory from actual robot start state. RobotConfig.fromGUISettings() reads settings.json so mass/MOI/COF/motor/current-limit live in one place. Emits DriveFeedforwards (per-module force) that map 1:1 onto Phoenix 6 ApplyRobotSpeeds.withWheelForceFeedforwardsX/Y. Rich trigger API on PathPlannerAuto (event, beforeEvent, distanceFromEvent, distanceFromEventEnd, pointTowardsZone, activePath, nearFieldPosition(AutoFlipped), inFieldArea(AutoFlipped), timeElapsed, timeRange, condition, isRunning). SendableChooser generation via buildAutoChooser()/buildAutoChooserWithOptionsModifier(Function<Stream<PathPlannerAuto>,Stream<PathPlannerAuto>>). Ships SwerveSetpointGenerator (254-derived) and PPHolonomicDriveController with static feedback overrides (overrideXFeedback/overrideYFeedback/overrideXYFeedback/overrideRotationFeedback/clearFeedbackOverrides).
landscape.gaps: Trajectories are spline+profile, not time-optimal — measurably slower than Choreo on the same waypoints for aggressive autos. NamedCommands is a global string->Command registry, which is a hidden-coupling footgun (a NamedCommand sharing requirements with the auto group cancels the group). No first-class branching inside an .auto file — dynamic autos must be built in Java, abandoning the GUI. Event markers are the only in-path coordination primitive at the .auto level; the richer trigger API only exists once you wrap in PathPlannerAuto in Java. Pathfinding is non-deterministic under AdvantageKit replay unless you swap in LocalADStarAK. Choreo trajectories loaded via fromChoreoTrajectory cannot be regenerated to match actual start state.

Per release notes 2026 had no major API changes over 2025; the 2025 release was the ground-up trajectory generation rewrite.
landscape.integrationShape:
RobotConfig cfg = RobotConfig.fromGUISettings();
AutoBuilder.configure(
    robotState::getPose,
    robotState::resetPose,
    drive::getRobotRelativeSpeeds,
    (speeds, ff) -> drive.setControl(
        applyRobotSpeeds.withSpeeds(speeds)
            .withWheelForceFeedforwardsX(ff.robotRelativeForcesXNewtons())
            .withWheelForceFeedforwardsY(ff.robotRelativeForcesYNewtons())),
    new PPHolonomicDriveController(new PIDConstants(5,0,0), new PIDConstants(5,0,0)),
    cfg,
    () -> DriverStation.getAlliance().orElse(Alliance.Blue) == Alliance.Red,
    drive);
NamedCommands.registerCommands(Map.of("intake", superstructure.request(INTAKE), "score", superstructure.request(SCORE_L4)));
Pathfinding.setPathfinder(new LocalADStarAK()); // AdvantageKit users, before warmup
FollowPathCommand.warmupCommand().schedule();   // in robotInit

landscape.doesWell: Time-optimal trajectory optimization respecting real dynamics constraints; faster wall-clock autos than spline-and-profile for the same waypoints. Constraint set: Stop Point, Max Velocity, Max Acceleration, Max Angular Velocity, Point At, Keep In Circle/Rectangle/Lane, Keep Out Circle, applied at waypoint scope, segment scope, or both. Waypoint types: Pose (translation+rotation), Translation, Empty (cannot be an endpoint). AutoFactory/AutoRoutine/AutoTrajectory give the best-in-class mechanism-coordination surface in FRC: AutoTrajectory exposes active(), inactive(), done(), doneDelayed(double), doneFor(double), recentlyDone(), atTime(double), atTime(String eventName), atTimeBeforeEnd(double), atTranslation(Translation2d|String, tol), atPose(Pose2d|String, transTol, rotTol), collectEventTimes(String), collectEventPoses(String), chain(AutoTrajectory), spawnCmd(), resetOdometry(), getInitialPose()/getFinalPose(), and mirrorX()/mirrorY()/rotateAround(). AutoRoutine adds anyActive(...), allInactive(...), anyDone(...), anyDoneDelayed(int cycles, ...), observe(BooleanSupplier), cmd(), cmd(BooleanSupplier finish), idle(), kill(), reset(), poll(), loop(). AutoChooser does lazy generation: addRoutine(String, Supplier<AutoRoutine>), addCmd(String, Supplier<Command>), selectedCommandScheduler(). Split waypoints let one .traj be addressed as sub-trajectories by index. Generated Java files from the GUI have no ChoreoLib dependency.
landscape.gaps: No pathfinding / on-the-fly path generation whatsoever — everything is pre-baked. No ability to regenerate from actual start state, so a bumped start pose means the follower fights a stale feedforward. Choreo does not support PathPlanner-style zoned events (markers are instants only). Optimizer failures are opaque to students; solve times can be long and require regeneration on every robot-config change. No GUI-level auto sequencing at all — composition is 100% Java. .traj loading is blocking and must happen at startup.
landscape.version2026: Choreo v2026.0.3 (2026-04-06). 2026.0.0 was the season release; 2026.0.1 (2026-01-12) was macOS/vendordep fixes with ChoreoLib unchanged; 2026.0.2 (2026-03-02) moved Java codegen to the backend enabling CLI codegen and added an alliance-flipped trajectory view; 2026.0.3 added mirrorX()/mirrorY()/rotateAround() trajectory flipping, a Java warmup command, and solver angular-acceleration handling in the swerve equation (Sleipnir 0.5.1). Vendordep: https://choreo.autos/lib/ChoreoLib2026.json

landscape.doesWell: Command composition primitives every auto architecture is built on: Commands.sequence/parallel/deadline/race/either/select/repeatingSequence/waitUntil/waitSeconds/runOnce/defer/print, Command.withTimeout/raceWith/deadlineFor/alongWith/andThen/finallyDo, Trigger + EventLoop (which ChoreoLib's AutoRoutine is built on), RobotModeTriggers.autonomous(), SendableChooser, ProfiledPIDController, TrapezoidProfile, HolonomicDriveController, LTVUnicycleController (used by ChoreoLib's differential example), SwerveDriveKinematics, SwerveDrivePoseEstimator.

Constructor takes (Trajectory<SwerveSample>, Supplier<Optional<Double>> omegaOverride, Drive, BooleanSupplier mirror) — the omega override is how shoot-on-the-move works during a path (launchOnTheMoveOmega()). AutoSelector extends VirtualSubsystem with addRoutine(String name, List<AutoQuestion> questions, Command command) where AutoQuestion is a record(String question, List<AutoQuestionResponse> responses), publishing up to 6 dependent question dropdowns to NetworkTables and freezing responses once auto is enabled. AutoCommands.java shows dynamic composition: Commands.repeatingSequence of intake/return/fire cycles, .raceWith(Commands.waitUntil(() -> withinTolerance(pose, 0.25, rot))) to time mechanism actions against pose rather than time, SalesmanSolver (TSP over detected game pieces) and getDynamicBounds() that expands the search region based on ObjectDetection.getInstance().getRobotTranslations() (opponent robots seen by vision).
