landscape.doesWell: Deterministic log replay: records ALL inputs flowing into robot code each loop, so a match can be re-run in the simulator and NEW log fields added retroactively. `@AutoLog` on an `IOInputs` class generates the (de)serializer; `Logger.processInputs("Drive/Module0", inputs)` swaps between real hardware and the log transparently. 2026 adds unit metadata for unit-aware AdvantageScope graphing, NetworkTables client logging (auto-detects dashboards/coprocessors + IPs), console/exception capture during Replay Watch, `LoggedMechanism2d.generate3dMechanism` for 3D articulated components, and an updated TalonFX(S)/CANdi swerve template.
landscape.gaps: Java-only. Forces the IO-layer discipline on every subsystem (high boilerplate for a 10-student team). Determinism is fragile — any HAL/clock/thread/HashMap-ordering call outside an IO layer silently breaks replay, and nothing checks this for you. No opinionated superstructure, auto, or vision layer; it is purely plumbing.
landscape.version2026: AdvantageKit 2026.x (supports WPILib 2026). PyKit (Team 1757) is the Python equivalent.
landscape.integrationShape: Rootstock should require AdvantageKit rather than re-implement logging: `public class RootstockRobot extends LoggedRobot` that in its ctor calls `Logger.recordMetadata(...)`, picks `WPILOGWriter("/U/logs")` + `NT4Publisher()` in REAL mode and `WPILOGReader(LogFileUtil.findReplayLog())` in REPLAY, then `Logger.start()`. Provide `@RootstockIO` = thin re-export of `@AutoLog` plus a compile-time/runtime `ReplaySafety.assertNoHalCalls()` check that AdvantageKit does not offer.

landscape.doesWell: The de-facto match 3D replay + mechanism visualization tool. 3D Field tab with CAD-based robot models, Mechanism tab, swerve module vectors, joystick display, synchronized match video, console, statistics, CSV/WPILOG export, heatmaps (new 2026), and AdvantageScope XR (AR viewing, stability improved for iOS/iPadOS 26). Custom assets are a folder named `TYPE_NAME` (`Robot_Darwin`, `Field3d_2026`) containing `config.json` + `model.glb`, with articulated parts as `model_0.glb`, `model_1.glb`… driven by a logged `Pose3d[]`; components declare `zeroedRotations` / `zeroedPosition`.
landscape.gaps: Asset authoring is manual and error-prone (hand-written config.json, hand-exported glTF, manual index↔Pose3d correspondence). No automatic generation of the Pose3d[] from a kinematic chain — every team re-writes that math. AdvantageScope Lite (browser version served from the robot) is 2027/Systemcore-only, so on-robot browsing does not exist in 2026.
landscape.version2026: AdvantageScope 2026 (v26.x); Lite ships only in v27.x on Systemcore.
landscape.integrationShape: Do NOT build a viewer. Build the asset+pose generator: `RobotViz.named("Rootstock").component("elevatorStage1", () -> new Transform3d(0,0,elevator.getHeightMeters()*0.5, Rotation3d.kZero)).component("arm", () -> ...).publish("Mechanism3d")` which logs a `Pose3d[]` in exactly component order and `viz.exportAssets(Path.of("ascope_assets/Robot_Rootstock"))` which writes a valid `config.json` with matching `model_N.glb` slots.

landscape.doesWell: The closest existing thing to Rootstock and the single best prior art to study. Swerve starter library on AdvantageKit + PathPlanner + PhotonLib with: an abstract `RobotConfig` + `RobotType` enum pattern so one codebase drives comp bot / practice bot / sim; drive-to-pose and rotate-to-angle closed-loop commands; on-the-fly move-to-pose; SysId routines selectable from a chooser; shipped `AdvantageScope.json` / `AdvantageScopeTuning.json` layouts; and — uniquely — written *pedagogy*: documented guides for State Machines (rationale, diagrams, best practices), Tuning Odometry ("good, better, best" approaches), Subsystem Testing and Tuning, Tuning Drivetrain and Auto, and Coordinate Systems. Ships tuning autos (straight-line distance, 180° rotation, oval-with-pause) specifically to measure odometry error.
landscape.gaps: Drivetrain-centric; no superstructure state-machine engine, no scoring-action/macro layer, no shoot-on-the-move, no mechanism 3D viz generator, no PID-tuning teaching app. CTRE-first (Kraken/Falcon + CANcoder + Pigeon); REV support is second-class. Docs live in Google Docs, not versioned with the code. No Choreo integration.
landscape.version2026: HuskieRobotics/frc-software-2026 (season repo) + 3061-lib releases; 2025.0.0 discussion at github.com/HuskieRobotics/3061-lib/discussions/132
landscape.integrationShape: Adopt the config pattern verbatim: `public abstract class RootstockRobotConfig { public abstract double getWheelRadiusMeters(); ... }` selected by `Constants.ROBOT` enum; ship `DefaultRobotConfig` full of `// FIXME` markers. Adopt the tuning-auto idea as `OdometryReport.squareTest(Meters.of(3))` returning measured closure error.

landscape.doesWell: GUI path authoring with Bézier curves, decoupled holonomic rotation, event markers, `AutoBuilder` full-auto generation, real-time path-following telemetry, and on-the-fly pathfinding with AD*. Broadest adoption; easiest onramp for a new team.
landscape.gaps: Not time-optimal (Choreo is). 2026 was an intentional freeze: "no major changes of note for 2026 besides the addition of the 2026 field image… hold off on major changes for the 2027 switch to SystemCore" — so expect an API break in 2027.
landscape.version2026: PathPlanner 2026.1.2 (user is already on this)
landscape.integrationShape: Wrap, don't replace: `AutoLibrary.builder().drive(drive).pathplanner(robotConfig).flipForAlliance(true).build()` internally calls `AutoBuilder.configure(pose::get, pose::reset, drive::getChassisSpeeds, drive::runVelocity, controller, config, allianceFlipSupplier, drive)` once, and registers every `ScoringAction` in the library as a NamedCommand automatically so the GUI event dropdown is pre-populated.

landscape.doesWell: Time-optimal trajectory generation with real physical constraints (motor torque, mass, MOI). 2026 API is trigger-driven and composes cleanly: `AutoRoutine r = factory.newRoutine("x"); AutoTrajectory t = r.trajectory("leg1"); r.active().onTrue(Commands.sequence(t.resetOdometry(), t.cmd())); t.atTime("intake").onTrue(intake.cmd()); t.done().onTrue(next.cmd());` New for 2026: `AutoRoutine.trajectory(String)` is the preferred loader (replacing `AutoFactory.trajectory(name, routine)`), `AutoRoutine.observe(BooleanSupplier)` for routine-scoped Triggers, and alliance-aware `resetOdometry` on both `AutoFactory` and `AutoTrajectory`.
landscape.gaps: Generation is offline/slow; no in-match replanning. Two competing auto DSLs (this vs PathPlanner's `AutoBuilder`) is a real cognitive tax on a small team. Like PathPlanner, 2026 was a hold year with big changes queued for 2027.
landscape.version2026: Choreo 2026.x; vendordep JSON at https://choreo.autos/lib/ChoreoLib2026.json
landscape.integrationShape: One `AutoLibrary` façade over both: `autos.routine("3piece").leg("Start_to_A").atMarker("prep", superstructure.goalCommand(L4)).onDone(scoreL4).leg("A_to_Source").build()` compiles to ChoreoLib triggers when `.choreo()` was declared and to PathPlanner `AutoBuilder` + NamedCommands when `.pathplanner()` was — same team-facing code either way.

landscape.doesWell: Open-source, vendor-neutral coprocessor vision. `PhotonPoseEstimator(AprilTagFieldLayout, Transform3d robotToCam)` with 9 `PoseStrategy` options; `MULTI_TAG_PNP_ON_COPROCESSOR` recommended, plus `PNP_DISTANCE_TRIG_SOLVE` and `CONSTRAINED_SOLVEPNP` which require calling `addHeadingData()` every frame. Returns `Optional<EstimatedRobotPose>` (Pose3d + timestamp). 2026: object-detection model management rewritten (models now in the SQLite settings DB, exportable/importable; upload model + type labels/width/height/version instead of SSH), a Colab notebook for model conversion, Rubik Pi 3 support, a shipped FUEL detection model, and configurable target counts up to 127.
landscape.gaps: Teams must own calibration, camera mounting transforms, and std-dev modeling themselves. Multi-camera arbitration is left to the team (2910 had to write "automatic selection of optimal camera to relocalize from"). Per-strategy heading-data requirements are a common footgun.
landscape.version2026: PhotonVision 2026.1.1 (user's version); latest line 2026.3.x
landscape.integrationShape: `RootstockCamera pv = Photon.multiTag("front", ROBOT_TO_FRONT_CAM).withHeadingSource(pose::getRotation).withStdDevModel(StdDevModels.distanceScaled(0.4, 0.05));` — the wrapper owns calling `addHeadingData()` so the strategy footgun disappears.

landscape.doesWell: Zero-setup localization. `LimelightHelpers.SetRobotOrientation("limelight", yawDeg, 0,0,0,0,0)` then `LimelightHelpers.PoseEstimate mt2 = LimelightHelpers.getBotPoseEstimate_wpiBlue_MegaTag2("limelight")` → feed `addVisionMeasurement(mt2.pose, mt2.timestampSeconds)`. MegaTag2 "eliminate[s] the pose ambiguity problem" and gives good single-tag estimates from any perspective. Docs' recommended rejection rules: reject if `mt2.tagCount == 0` or `Math.abs(gyro.getRate()) > 360` deg/s; recommended std devs `VecBuilder.fill(0.7, 0.7, 9999999)` — i.e. never trust vision rotation.
landscape.gaps: Requires a correct yaw fed in every loop, and the doc example feeds the *estimator's own* rotation back in, which is a latent feedback loop if your estimator ever accepts vision rotation. Requires an uploaded .fmap and a configured camera-in-robot-space pose. Closed-source pipeline; single-vendor lock-in per camera.
landscape.version2026: Limelight 4 hardware is the 2025/2026 elite default (1678 ran two LL4s in 2025 and one LL4 in 2026)
landscape.integrationShape: `RootstockCamera ll = Limelight.megaTag2("limelight-front").fedBy(pose::getGyroRotationOnly);` — the wrapper enforces gyro-only yaw (never the fused rotation), applies the tagCount/gyro-rate rejections, and sets rotation std dev to ∞ so a user cannot create the feedback loop.

landscape.doesWell: Physics-engine robot simulation via the dyn4j 2D rigid-body engine: real forces and collisions between robots, field elements and game pieces, plus projectile simulation for launched pieces. Ships FRC2026 REBUILT field/game-piece updates and AdvantageKit swerve templates for both REV SparkMax/Flex and CTRE. Included in YAGSL.
landscape.gaps: 2D physics only (elevator/arm dynamics still need WPILib `ElevatorSim`/`SingleJointedArmSim`). Fidelity of intake/scoring interactions is approximate. Adds a nontrivial dependency and CPU load. Not officially blessed by WPILib.
landscape.version2026: Built against WPILib 2026.2.1, with "FRC2026 Game Rebuilt" updates
landscape.integrationShape: `SimWorld world = SimWorld.forGame(Game.REBUILT_2026).withRobot(SimRobot.swerve(driveConfig, Kilograms.of(55))).withIntake(intakeGeometry).withLauncher(ShotSim.projectile(launchCalculator));` — Rootstock selects `DriveIOMapleSim` vs `DriveIOTalonFX` from `Constants.mode`, so a student can run a full match on a laptop with no robot.

landscape.doesWell: Best-in-class motor control + the generated swerve project (`TunerConstants`, `SwerveDrivetrain`). New for 2026: a **LinearPath API** (linear path between two poses with constant velocity and acceleration limits) and a **WheelForceCalculator** that computes wheel force feedforwards for a target robot acceleration / ΔChassisSpeeds given robot mass — directly useful for traction-limited, skid-free driving. `DifferentialMechanism`/`SimpleDifferentialMechanism` reworked to take `DifferentialMotorConstants`. Phoenix Tuner can now control and plot multiple devices simultaneously and plot Hoot logs directly (beta).
landscape.gaps: `<Device>(int id, String canbus)` constructors are deprecated and removed in 2027 — use `<Device>(int id, CANBus canbus)`. `Configs.hpp` split (C++). Generated `TunerConstants` fights AdvantageKit's IO pattern (2910 had to reconcile CTRE swerve API + AdvantageKit). Hoot logs are not replayable by AdvantageKit.
landscape.version2026: Phoenix 6 26.x (user's version)
landscape.integrationShape: Expose CTRE's new primitives rather than hiding them: `drive.setTractionLimited(chassisSpeeds)` internally uses `WheelForceCalculator` feedforwards; `AutoAlign.linear(targetPose)` delegates to the Phoenix 6 `LinearPath` API when the drivetrain is a Phoenix swerve, falling back to a Rootstock profile otherwise.

landscape.doesWell: 2026: Epilogue logging now handles superclass fields and protobuf-serializable types; `Subsystem.idle()`; `Preferences.getNetworkTable()`; X44 and Minion motor definitions; Eigen 5.0.0. WPILib also ships genuinely good *interactive* controls-tuning tutorials (flywheel velocity, turret position, vertical arm, elevator with motion profiling) that teach an "exponential search" tuning method (×2 until overshoot, then bisect) and let students toggle gaussian system noise.
landscape.gaps: 2027 is the largest break since the cRIO and lands before Rootstock would mature: roboRIO → **Systemcore**, Java 17 → **Java 25**, packages `edu.wpi.first` → **`org.wpilib`** (C++ `frc::` → `wpi::`), **Commands v3** coroutine framework, `XboxController`/`PS4Controller`/etc. collapsed into one `Gamepad`, `MotorController.set()` → `setThrottle()`, `stopMotor()` → `disable()`, NetworkTables v3 removed, "Test" mode renamed "Utility", Gradle 9.4.1, ZGC default, and **Shuffleboard, SmartDashboard, PathWeaver and RobotBuilder deleted**. 2026 projects must be re-imported to build for 2027. Relays, analog outputs and SPI are gone from the hardware.
landscape.version2026: WPILib 2026.x on Java 17; 2027.0.0-alpha-6 already published
landscape.integrationShape: Ship Rootstock 2026 against `edu.wpi.first` + Commands v2, but keep every public API expressed in terms of `Supplier`/`Consumer`/`Command` and your own `RootstockState`/`RootstockCamera` types, never leaking `XboxController`, `Shuffleboard`, or NT3. Plan a `rootstock-2027` branch that swaps the Command type and package roots; the superstructure graph, solvers, and vision layer should port unchanged.

landscape.doesWell: The most widely used driver-station dashboard in FRC; Flutter-based, designed for behind-the-glass. 2026 adds more platform support (Windows/macOS/Linux/**Web**), more data-viewing capability, and SystemCore support — so it survives the 2027 Shuffleboard/SmartDashboard deletion.
landscape.gaps: Driver-facing only; not an analysis or replay tool, and no mechanism/3D visualization. Layout is hand-built per season.
landscape.version2026: Elastic 2026.x
landscape.integrationShape: Rootstock should *emit* an Elastic-compatible layout: `RootstockDashboard.publishDriverLayout()` writes the NT topics (auto chooser, alliance, superstructure state, vision health, battery, alerts) with stable names plus a generated `elastic-layout.json`, so a rookie team gets a competent driver dashboard with zero clicking.

landscape.doesWell: JSON-configured swerve that works across vendors and module types with minimal code; explicitly aimed at teams of all experience levels; bundles maple-sim.
landscape.gaps: JSON-config approach diverges from the IO/replay pattern; less transparent for students learning what the code does; no superstructure/auto/vision layer.
landscape.version2026: YAGSL 2026
landscape.integrationShape: Treat as an alternative drivetrain backend, not a dependency: `RootstockDrive.fromYagsl(swerveDrive)` adapting `getPose/resetPose/getChassisSpeeds/drive` so YAGSL teams can still use Rootstock's superstructure, actions, and vision layers.

landscape.doesWell: Mature Java graph library; 6328 uses `DefaultDirectedGraph<SuperstructureState, EdgeCommand>` directly for the superstructure. Gives free BFS/Dijkstra/A*, cycle detection, and connectivity checks.
landscape.gaps: Extra dependency to vendordep/shade for a roboRIO deploy; generic API is verbose; nothing FRC-specific.
landscape.version2026: JGraphT 1.5.x (as vendored by 6328)
landscape.integrationShape: Either shade JGraphT or ship ~150 lines of A*/BFS (254 wrote their own: `List<N> AStarSolver.solve(N start, N goal, Heuristic<N> h, Neighbors<N> n)` with an `Edge<N>{N neighbor; double cost;}`). Recommend the latter — one file, no dependency, and it is readable by a student.

landscape.tool: Team 254 FRC-2025-Public (reference architecture, not a library)
landscape.doesWell: The most complete published superstructure design. `SuperstructureStateMachine` holds `Map<SuperstructureState, List<StateTransition>> graph`, `List<StateTransition>[][] precomputedPaths`, `Map<String,Double> transitionCostMap`, and `SuperstructureState currentState/desiredState/futureDesiredState`. Transitions are auto-generated (`autoGenerateTransitions()` reads each state's `allowedNextStates()`), costs are *measured on the real robot* and persisted to `transition_costs.txt` (`loadTransitionCosts()`, `buildCharacterizationCommand()`), interlocks live in `isTransitionBlocked(StateTransition)`, and blocked routes fall back to `computeDynamicTransitionPath(from, to)`. Gateway states (`CLEAR_ELEVATOR_CROSSBEAM`, `INTERMEDIATE_BARGE`) implement collision avoidance by clamping the wrist angle and restricting `allowedNextStates()` to a single exit. Repo also contains `viz/`, `simulation/`, `factories/`, `controlboard/`.
landscape.gaps: Not packaged as a library; game-specific (`CoralStateTracker`, reef-face helpers `getClosestFace()`, `isCloserToLeftFeeder()` live inside the state machine); relies on 254-internal utilities (`ChezySequenceCommandGroup`). Nothing is documented for outside consumption.
landscape.version2026: FRC-2025-Public (GradleRIO 2025.3.2). No FRC-2026-Public repo exists as of Aug 2026 — UNVERIFIED whether one will be released.
landscape.integrationShape: This is the single design to generalize. Rootstock's superstructure engine = 254's structure minus the game specifics: measured transition costs, auto-generated edges, gateway states, `isTransitionBlocked` interlocks, precomputed all-pairs paths.

landscape.doesWell: Best published 2026-season code. `subsystems/{drive,hopper,hubcounter,kicker,launcher,leds,rollers,sensors,slamtake,vision}`; `commands/{DriveCommands, DriveToPose, DriveTrajectory, SimTrajectory, CompactingCommands, auto/}`; `util/{LoggedTunableNumber, VirtualSubsystem, LoggedTracer, SwitchableChooser, ContinuousConditionalCommand, EqualsUtil, FuelSim, geometry/, logging/, vts/}`; plus a `salesman/` package (`SalesmanSolver`, `SalesmanSolverIO`, `SalesmanCommands`, `SalesAssociate`) that is a travelling-salesman optimizer for auto route ordering, an `energy/` package for power budgeting, and `util/vts/{ChoreoJSON, ChoreoLauncher, GenerateTrajectories}` that generates Choreo trajectories programmatically instead of drawing them by hand. `VisionIONorthstar` is their own coprocessor pipeline behind a plain `VisionIO` interface. CD consensus: "Luckily for many turret bots, 6328 posted some VERY functional code that handles [shoot on the move]."
landscape.gaps: Written for their robot and their process; no stable API, no versioning, MIT-licensed copy-paste only. Northstar is not a product. Requires full AdvantageKit buy-in.
landscape.version2026: 2026 season, robot "Darwin" / "Darwin 2.0"
landscape.integrationShape: Lift patterns, not files: `LoggedTunableNumber`, `VirtualSubsystem`, `LoggedTracer` (loop-time attribution), `SwitchableChooser`, and the `DriveToPose` FF-ramp structure should all have Rootstock equivalents with the same semantics and better docs.

landscape.doesWell: 2910: AdvantageKit + CTRE swerve API + a documented "custom finite state machine architecture" with a central `Superstructure` orchestrator; "fully automated coral scoring on all levels", automated algae pickup, automated climb; "single driver/controller setup with bindings switching based on robot state"; "vision relocalization with custom algorithm" including "automatic selection of optimal camera to relocalize from"; `.github/workflows` CI and `./gradlew test` JUnit. Credits code adapted from 254 and 6328. 1678 C2026-Public "Limestone": `shooting/{targeting, driveplanner, shootingplanner, regressions, setpoints, trends, verification}` — note **`verification`** and **`trends`**, i.e. the robot self-checks shot quality and tracks it over time; one Limelight 4; one primary controller plus a debug controller; `frc/lib/io` IO interfaces and `lib/sim`.
landscape.gaps: Both are season repos, not libraries. 1678's targeting layer is deeply game-specific. Neither documents its internals for outsiders.
landscape.version2026: 2910: 2025 season (Java 17+). 1678: C2026-Public, 2026 season.
landscape.integrationShape: Two ideas worth stealing wholesale into Rootstock: (a) `CameraArbiter.best(List<RootstockCamera>, Pose2d)` scoring cameras by tag count / distance / view angle, and (b) a `ShotVerification` module that logs predicted-vs-observed outcome per shot and surfaces a running success rate — nothing in the ecosystem does this.

landscape.doesWell: Public EPA/OPR data that makes the elite-vs-average gap measurable rather than anecdotal, and lets a team benchmark its own auto/teleop/endgame components against a target percentile.
landscape.gaps: EPA is a black box relative to *why* a team scores; converges slowly early season (a top team like 2056 sat at 142.3 EPA / 35th worldwide early in 2026 purely from insufficient matches).
landscape.version2026: Statbotics API v3 (UNVERIFIED exact version as of Aug 2026)
landscape.integrationShape: Out of scope for a robot-code library, but a `rootstock-tools` CLI could pull a team's Statbotics component EPAs and compare them against the team's own log-derived cycle stats: `rootstock stats --team 8793 --event 2026xyz`.

capabilities.capability: #1 — Zero-boilerplate replay-safe logging + one-line AdvantageKit setup (`RootstockRobot`)
capabilities.whyItMatters: The single highest impact-per-hour practice for a small team. A 10-student team with 6 hrs/week cannot afford to debug at the field by re-running matches; log replay converts one broken match into an offline debugging session on a laptop at home. Community consensus for a "world class software team" is exactly: unit tests + AdvantageKit + full sim (chiefdelphi.com/t/513371). But the IO-layer boilerplate is what stops small teams from adopting it — remove that and this becomes nearly free.
capabilities.prerequisites: AdvantageKit 2026 vendordep; a Gradle plugin (or an annotation-processor/ErrorProne check) for the replay-safety scan.

capabilities.capability: #2 — Declarative superstructure state graph with auto-routing, measured transition costs, and interlocks
capabilities.whyItMatters: This is the one thing that most separates elite multi-mechanism robots and is almost never attempted by small teams, because writing 30 hand-coded arm/elevator sequences is intractable at 6 hrs/week. 254 and 6328 both solved it as a graph search; nobody has packaged it. A declarative graph also directly satisfies the user's "mechanisms easy to create and modify" requirement: adding a state is 3 lines, and the library recomputes every legal route and every collision check. It converts the hardest software problem in FRC into configuration.
capabilities.apiSketch:
public enum SuperState implements RootstockState { STOW, INTAKE, L1, L2, L3, L4, CLEAR_CROSSBEAM, CLIMB }

Superstructure<SuperState> sup = Superstructure.of(SuperState.class)
  .axis("elevator", elevator::setHeight, elevator::getHeight, Tolerance.of(Meters.of(0.02)))
  .axis("wrist",    wrist::setAngle,    wrist::getAngle,    Tolerance.of(Degrees.of(2)))
  .at(STOW, "elevator", 0.00, "wrist", Degrees.of(-15))
  .at(L4,   "elevator", 1.55, "wrist", Degrees.of(52))
  .gateway(CLEAR_CROSSBEAM)                      // 254 pattern: only legal exit from restricted regions
  .only(SuperState.INTERMEDIATE_L4, SuperState.L4)  // == 254 allowedNextStates() restriction
  .interlock(() -> gripper.hasAlgae(), Set.of(L1, L2))
  .forbidRegion(new BoxConstraint("wrist", Degrees.of(-40), Degrees.of(10))
                  .whenever("elevator", Meters.of(0.30), Meters.of(0.55)))  // declarative collision zone
  .estopOn(() -> !elevator.encoderConnected())
  .build();

sup.setGoal(L4);                    // request/goal; library BFS/A*s the cheapest legal path
sup.atGoal(L4);                     // Trigger
sup.isStable();                     // 254's !transitioning
Command c = sup.goalCommand(L4);

// Cost measurement made free (254 does this manually via transition_costs.txt):
Command cal = sup.characterizeTransitions();   // drives every edge, times it, writes /home/lvuser/rootstock/transition_costs.json
// Static analysis at build time:
sup.report();  // -> unreachable states, states with no path home, edges violating a forbidRegion
capabilities.prerequisites: A ~150-line A*/BFS (`List<N> solve(N start, N goal, Heuristic<N>, Neighbors<N>)` per 254's AStarSolver) — no JGraphT dependency needed. Requires the axis abstraction to be generic over any mechanism with a setpoint + measurement.

capabilities.capability: #3 — Vision-assisted single-button scoring actions that prep during travel
capabilities.whyItMatters: Cycle time is where the elite/average gap is visibly cashed in — "the difference between an average bot and a great bot last year could largely be defined by placement time, which was part mechanical, but in most part software related" (chiefdelphi.com/t/516134). 2910 shipped fully automated scoring on all levels; 254 gates every binding through modal controls. For a small team this multiplies the value of a mediocre driver, which is exactly the leverage they need. Prepping the superstructure *while driving* (rather than after arriving) is typically worth 1–2 s per cycle and is trivial once #2 exists.
capabilities.apiSketch:
ScoringAction scoreL4 = ScoringAction.named("L4")
   .target(() -> FieldTargets.nearest(pose.get(), FieldTargets.L4_POSES))
   .prepareWhenWithin(Meters.of(2.0), sup.goalCommand(SuperState.L4))   // overlap travel + mechanism motion
   .align(AutoAlign.to(target).withTolerance(Meters.of(0.02), Degrees.of(1.5)))
   .requireBeforeRelease(sup.atGoal(SuperState.L4), align.atGoal(), pose.isTrusted())
   .release(endEffector.eject().withTimeout(0.3))
   .retreat(sup.goalCommand(SuperState.STOW))
   .abortIf(() -> driver.getLeftY() > 0.5)      // driver always retains authority
   .build();

ControlBoard board = ControlBoard.modal(driver)
   .mode("SCORE", m -> m.rightBumper().whileTrue(scoreL4.command()))
   .mode("MANUAL", m -> m.rightBumper().whileTrue(endEffector.eject()))  // 254 CORALMANUAL escape hatch
   .build();
capabilities.prerequisites: #2 superstructure, #5 auto-align, #4 pose engine. Must ship with a mandatory manual mode — elite teams all keep one.

capabilities.capability: #4 — `PoseEngine`: opinionated odometry + multi-camera vision fusion with built-in rejection and error measurement
capabilities.whyItMatters: Every downstream capability (auto-align, auto, score-on-the-move) is worthless if the pose is 30 cm off, and small teams routinely never measure their odometry error at all. 6328 does not use `SwerveDrivePoseEstimator` — they run their own closed-form Kalman update in `RobotState` with a 2 s `TimeInterpolatableBuffer`, tilt-scaled translation from IMU pitch/roll, and a backup gyro. Making that the default, plus a one-command wheel-radius characterization and a printed error report, is the highest-leverage 'invisible' upgrade available.
capabilities.prerequisites: Requires a real odometry thread (Phoenix 6 `BaseStatusSignal.waitForAll` at 250 Hz, or REV's periodic frames). Skid detection interacting with pose estimation is genuinely hard — CD notes it is "pretty hard to use skid detection with the WPILib SwerveDrivePoseEstimator" — so implement it as a std-dev inflation, not a rejection.

capabilities.capability: #5 — `AutoAlign`: profiled drive-to-pose with feedforward ramping and driver override
capabilities.whyItMatters: The most reused command in every elite codebase and the one small teams write worst (usually a raw P controller that oscillates). 6328's version is a specific, non-obvious structure: separate `PIDController` for translation and `ProfiledPIDController` for heading, constraints rebuilt every loop from tunable numbers, and — the key trick — a feedforward scaler that ramps in linearly between a min and max error radius so the robot does not slam or creep: `clamp((driveErrorAbs - ffMinRadius)/(ffMaxRadius - ffMinRadius), 0, 1)`.
capabilities.prerequisites: #4 PoseEngine. Optionally delegate to Phoenix 6 2026's new LinearPath API when the drivetrain is a CTRE swerve.

capabilities.capability: #6 — Sim-first bring-up: auto-selected sim IO layers + maple-sim world + a 'run a whole match on a laptop' entry point
capabilities.whyItMatters: This is the practice most directly aimed at the small team's real constraint: one robot, 6 hrs/week. Elite teams' advantage is substantially *robot-hours*, and simulation is the only way to buy those back. A team that can run its full auto and a scoring cycle in sim before the mechanism exists gets ~80% of the debugging value of a practice bot. maple-sim already provides dyn4j physics, game-piece collisions and projectile sim with 2026 REBUILT assets — this is integration, not invention.
capabilities.prerequisites: maple-sim dependency (WPILib 2026.2.1 baseline); WPILib `ElevatorSim`/`SingleJointedArmSim`/`FlywheelSim` for non-drivetrain axes; `SimHooks` time stepping for deterministic headless runs.

capabilities.capability: #7 — Unified auto layer over PathPlanner *and* Choreo, with auto-registered actions and alliance handling
capabilities.whyItMatters: Auto quality is the most reliably decisive software differentiator because it is fully deterministic and unaffected by driver skill — a small team can beat a better-driving team on auto alone. The two dominant tools have incompatible DSLs and both froze in 2026 pending 2027 SystemCore changes, so a thin façade protects the team from that churn. Auto-registering every `ScoringAction` as a PathPlanner NamedCommand / Choreo event removes the #1 rookie auto failure (typo'd marker names).
capabilities.prerequisites: PathPlanner 2026.1.2 and/or ChoreoLib 2026 vendordeps. Must expose the underlying `AutoFactory`/`AutoBuilder` so teams are never trapped by the façade.

capabilities.capability: #8 — `RootstockTuner`: guided, teaching-oriented on-robot tuning with saved gains
capabilities.whyItMatters: Explicitly requested, and genuinely missing. WPILib has excellent *browser* tuning tutorials (flywheel/turret/arm/elevator, with the 'exponential search' method: ×2 until overshoot, then bisect) but they are decoupled from the student's actual robot. SysId characterizes but does not teach. Phoenix Tuner X plots but is vendor-locked. A small team's real bottleneck is that one student knows how to tune and graduates. Encoding the workflow — pick mechanism type → run characterization → fit kS/kV/kA → suggested kP → live step-response overlay of expected vs actual → save to JSON — makes tuning transferable and repeatable.
capabilities.prerequisites: WPILib SysId routines (`SysIdRoutine`) for the data collection; a NetworkTables-backed web UI or an Elastic/AdvantageScope-compatible surface. Gains file must be readable by the robot code without redeploy. Note: 2027 removes Shuffleboard/SmartDashboard — build the UI on NT4 + a served web page, not on those.

capabilities.capability: #9 — `RobotViz`: declarative kinematic chain → logged `Pose3d[]` + generated AdvantageScope custom assets
capabilities.whyItMatters: Requested directly, and the manual path is a known time sink: hand-writing `config.json`, hand-exporting `.glb` per component, and hand-maintaining the index↔`Pose3d` correspondence. Beyond looking good, a correct 3D mechanism view is the fastest way to spot a wrong sign, a bad zero offset, or a collision that the state graph should have prevented — which makes it a debugging tool, not decoration.
capabilities.apiSketch:
RobotViz viz = RobotViz.named("Rootstock")
  .component("elevator_stage1", "assets/stage1.glb",
             () -> new Transform3d(0, 0, elevator.getHeightMeters() * 0.5, Rotation3d.kZero))
  .component("elevator_carriage", "assets/carriage.glb",
             () -> new Transform3d(0, 0, elevator.getHeightMeters(), Rotation3d.kZero))
  .component("wrist", "assets/wrist.glb",
             () -> new Transform3d(0.20, 0, elevator.getHeightMeters(),
                                   new Rotation3d(0, wrist.getAngleRad(), 0)))
  .camera("front", ROBOT_TO_FRONT_CAM)
  .gamePiece("fuel", () -> gripper.hasPiece() ? Optional.of(pieceTransform) : Optional.empty());

viz.publish("Mechanism3d");                       // logs Pose3d[] in component order every loop
viz.exportAssets(Path.of("ascope_assets/Robot_Rootstock"));  // writes config.json + copies model_N.glb
viz.assertConsistent();                            // fails the build if component count != Pose3d[] length

// Also: 2D for quick checks, delegating to AdvantageKit 2026
LoggedMechanism2d m2d = viz.as2d();
capabilities.prerequisites: AdvantageScope custom-asset schema (`config.json` with `components[]`, `zeroedRotations`, `zeroedPosition`; `model.glb` + `model_0.glb`…). AdvantageKit 2026's `LoggedMechanism2d.generate3dMechanism` covers part of this — wrap it rather than duplicating.

capabilities.capability: #10 — `ShotSolver`: generic score/shoot-on-the-move with iterative time-of-flight and setpoint derivatives
capabilities.whyItMatters: For 2026 REBUILT and any future shooter game this is the visible top-tier capability — CD's read of week 1 2026 was that "shoot on the move for both turrets and dumpers [is] becoming a key component for all competitive bots by worlds". 6328's `LaunchCalculator` shows the correct structure and it is fully game-agnostic: 20-iteration fixed-point solve on time of flight, an exponential drag model `(1 - exp(-tof*k))/k` applied to robot velocity, a ~30 ms phase delay for actuator lag, interpolating maps distance→{hoodAngle, flywheelSpeed, tof, kickerSpeed}, and a returned record carrying *velocities as well as positions* so hood/turret/drive lead the moving aim point. Ranked below odometry deliberately: SOTM on a 30 cm-error pose is worse than stopping to shoot.
capabilities.prerequisites: #4 PoseEngine with a trustworthy field-relative velocity. Requires the team to collect a distance→parameter table (ship a `ShotTableWizard` command that steps distances and records manually-confirmed makes).

capabilities.capability: #11 — `RobotConfig`/`RobotType` multi-robot configuration (practice bot / comp bot / sim / last year's bot)
capabilities.whyItMatters: 3061-lib's most quietly valuable feature and directly serves "easy to create and modify mechanisms." 2910 explicitly built a "configuration framework [that] enables running competition code on legacy robots for testing." For a one-robot team the equivalent win is running the *current* code on last year's chassis or in sim while this year's robot is in pieces — which is often the only way to get software hours during build season.
capabilities.prerequisites: None. Copy 3061-lib's pattern; add capability flags so partial robots boot cleanly.

capabilities.capability: #12 — `HealthMonitor` + pre-match self-test + structured alerts
capabilities.whyItMatters: Elite teams lose almost no matches to 'the robot didn't move'; small teams lose several per event. A scripted self-test (every motor spins the right direction, every encoder moves, CAN utilization sane, no device on a stale firmware, battery under load) run in the queue line converts an unwinnable match into a 2-minute pit fix. Nothing in the ecosystem packages this; teams re-write ad-hoc checklists every year.
capabilities.apiSketch:
HealthMonitor.register(drive, elevator, wrist, launcher, pose);

Command selfTest = HealthMonitor.selfTest()          // safe, low-power, bounded motion
   .check(Checks.canBusUtilizationBelow(0.60))
   .check(Checks.allDevicesConnected())
   .check(Checks.firmwareMatches(expectedVersions))
   .check(Checks.encoderRespondsTo(elevator::setVoltage, elevator::getVelocityMps, Volts.of(1.0)))
   .check(Checks.batterySagUnder(Volts.of(2.0)))
   .check(Checks.visionSeesTags(atLeast(1), Seconds.of(3)))
   .check(Checks.odometryMatchesVision(Meters.of(0.15)));

// Results go to WPILib Alert + NT + AdvantageScope console + the driver dashboard:
HealthMonitor.summary();   // "PASS 11/12 — WARN: rear-left steer encoder offset drifted 4.2 deg"
capabilities.prerequisites: WPILib `Alert` API (UNVERIFIED exact package path for 2026 — confirm `edu.wpi.first.wpilibj.Alert` before use). Needs per-vendor device introspection (Phoenix 6 `StatusSignal`/`getVersion`, REVLib faults).

capabilities.capability: #13 — `CycleStats`: automatic post-match cycle/performance analytics from the log
capabilities.whyItMatters: Elite teams know their cycle time distribution; average teams have opinions about it. Because Rootstock owns `ScoringAction`, `AutoAlign` and the superstructure graph, it can emit structured events for free and compute what teams currently reconstruct by hand from video: cycles per match, time-to-align, superstructure transition times vs. measured baseline, vision uptime, and auto success rate. This is the feedback loop that turns practice hours into improvement — the closest a library can get to substituting for practice discipline.
capabilities.prerequisites: #1 logging and #3 scoring actions must emit a stable event schema. Log parsing needs a WPILOG reader (AdvantageKit/AdvantageScope both ship one; a small standalone Java reader is ~300 lines).

capabilities.capability: #14 — Test + CI scaffolding that actually runs (`rootstock-test` + generated GitHub Actions)
capabilities.whyItMatters: The one practice the community names first for 'world class software team' status and the one small teams skip. The blocker is not willingness, it is that FRC unit testing has non-obvious mechanics: reset the `CommandScheduler` in `@BeforeEach`, never construct the whole `RobotContainer`, put button bindings in their own class with a static setup method so the event loop can be swapped, and step time with `SimHooks` rather than sleeping. Ship those as helpers and a template and the cost collapses.
capabilities.prerequisites: JUnit 5, WPILib `SimHooks`/`DriverStationSim`. The `ReplayAssert` idea depends on AdvantageKit replay determinism holding — see pitfalls.

capabilities.capability: #15 — Explicit 2027 migration story (Systemcore / Commands v3 / org.wpilib)
capabilities.whyItMatters: Rootstock is being designed in Aug 2026, three months before a WPILib release that renames every package, changes the language level to Java 25, replaces the command framework, and changes the robot controller hardware. A library that ignores this ships one usable season. Conversely, a library that publishes a credible 2027 plan becomes the *reason* small teams adopt it, because the migration is exactly the kind of work a 10-student team cannot absorb.
capabilities.prerequisites: Track wpilibsuite/allwpilib 2027 alphas (2027.0.0-alpha-6 as of Aug 2026) and the docs.wpilib.org/en/2027 site. Assume PathPlanner and Choreo both break in 2027 — keep #7's façade thin enough to re-point.

eliteTeamPractices: **The gap is measured, not felt.** Statbotics EPA analysis posted March 2026: the P90/P50 ratio rose from 1.38 (2018) to 2.35 (2025); the 90th percentile went from 1.57x the median (2016) to 2.35x (2025) while the 10th percentile fell from 0.62x to ~0.45x; and the top 10% of teams now hold ~23.6% of total EPA vs the bottom 50%'s 26.5% (they were 14.7% vs 41.5% in 2018). https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/a-look-at-the-widening-performance-gap-in-frc/516134

**Software is now the marginal differentiator, and specifically placement/cycle time.** From that same thread: "There was a mechanical revolution in FIRST... Now you are seeing a software revolution. To a bot, EVERY top team has superb programming skills. The difference between an average bot and a great bot last year could largely be defined by placement time, which was part mechanical, but in most part software related." For 2026 the named capability is shoot-on-the-move for both turrets and dumpers. https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/a-look-at-the-widening-performance-gap-in-frc/516134

**Superstructures are modeled as searched graphs, not hand-written sequences.** Team 254 (2025): `SuperstructureStateMachine` holds `Map<SuperstructureState, List<StateTransition>> graph`, auto-generates edges via `autoGenerateTransitions()` from each state's `allowedNextStates()`, precomputes all-pairs routes into `List<StateTransition>[][] precomputedPaths`, and searches with a generic `AStarSolver.solve(start, goal, heuristic, neighbors)` weighted by *measured* transition times persisted in `transition_costs.txt` (`loadTransitionCosts()`, `buildCharacterizationCommand()`). https://github.com/Team254/FRC-2025-Public/tree/main/src/main/java/com/team254/frc2025/subsystems/superstructure

**Collision avoidance is expressed as gateway states and restricted edge sets, not runtime geometry.** 254's `SuperstructureState` enum carries `elevatorHeightMeters` + `wristAngleRad` per state; `CLEAR_ELEVATOR_CROSSBEAM` is a special state with a `Function<RobotContainer, Command> commandSupplier` that clamps the wrist into a safe band, and `INTERMEDIATE_BARGE`/`STAGE_BARGE` restrict `allowedNextStates()` to a single legal exit so no path can cut through the collision zone. Interlocks (e.g. block coral states while holding algae) live in `isTransitionBlocked(StateTransition)`, with `computeDynamicTransitionPath()` as the fallback route. https://github.com/Team254/FRC-2025-Public

**6328 solves the same problem with an explicit directed graph plus BFS.** `private final Graph<SuperstructureState, EdgeCommand> graph = new DefaultDirectedGraph<>(EdgeCommand.class)` (JGraphT); edges are built with `EdgeCommand.builder().command(...)`; `setGoal()` runs `bfs(start, goal)` returning only the *next* immediate state; `isEdgeAllowed()` filters on algae possession (`AlgaeEdge.NO_ALGAE`) and proximity restrictions; `elevatorCrossMemberDangerHeight` constrains pivot angle and a `reefDangerState` blocks scoring states when too close. Disable/e-stop forces a return to STOW. https://github.com/Mechanical-Advantage/RobotCode2025Public/blob/main/src/main/java/org/littletonrobotics/frc2025/subsystems/superstructure/Superstructure.java

**Driver decisions are minimized by modal control boards, with a manual escape hatch always present.** 254's `ModalControls` has three modes (CORAL, ALGAECLIMB, CORALMANUAL); every binding is wrapped by `modeSpecific()` = `trigger.and(new Trigger(() -> this.currentMode == mode))`, so a single physical button means different things safely. 2910 shipped a "single driver/controller setup with bindings switching based on robot state"; 1678's 2026 robot Limestone runs "one primary controller handling all functionality, with a secondary debug controller." https://github.com/Team254/FRC-2025-Public + https://github.com/FRCTeam2910/2025CompetitionRobot-Public + https://github.com/frc1678/C2026-Public

**Full-automation of scoring is the norm at the top, not an experiment.** 2910's 2025 README lists "Fully automated coral scoring on all levels, and automated stacking of coral on L1", "Fully automated algae pickups off of the reef", and an "Automated climb sequence". 1678 ran vision-based reef alignment for autonomous scoring with two Limelight 4s (AprilTag + neural coral detection). https://github.com/FRCTeam2910/2025CompetitionRobot-Public + https://github.com/frc1678/C2025-Public

**Elite pose estimation is custom, not `SwerveDrivePoseEstimator`.** 6328's 2026 `RobotState` keeps separate `odometryPose` and `estimatedPose`, a 2.0 s `TimeInterpolatableBuffer<Pose2d>` plus a `TimeInterpolatableBuffer<Rotation3d>`, scales translational odometry by IMU pitch/roll to suppress motion while tilted, overrides the twist's rotation with gyro when available, accepts an optional **backup gyro**, and applies a closed-form Kalman correction with gain `stdDev / (stdDev + sqrt(stdDev * r))` in `addVisionObservation(VisionObservation)`. https://github.com/Mechanical-Advantage/RobotCode2026Public/blob/main/src/main/java/org/littletonrobotics/frc2026/RobotState.java

**Wheel radius is characterized, not measured with a ruler, and re-checked.** 6328's `DriveCommands.wheelRadiusCharacterization(Drive)` spins the robot in place (0.25 rad/s target, 0.05 rad/s² ramp, 1 s settle) and solves `wheelRadius = (gyroDelta * driveBaseRadius) / wheelDelta`; `feedforwardCharacterization(Drive)` ramps 0.1 V/s and least-squares fits kS and kV. Team 334's 2026 build thread describes adopting this and then validating with "low-acceleration translation-only tests, driven forward and back 1 meter without vision, measuring odometry to real life pose error" before moving to higher-acceleration tests with vision. https://github.com/Mechanical-Advantage/RobotCode2026Public/blob/main/src/main/java/org/littletonrobotics/frc2026/commands/DriveCommands.java + https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/frc-334-techknights-2026-build-thread-open-alliance/510072

**Skid/slip detection is an active elite topic and is deliberately handled as a weighting, not a hard reject.** Orbit 1690's 2024 software session on PoseTracking is the widely-cited origin; a 2026 CD writeup derives basic swerve skid detection from it; FRC 135's Consul framework implements 1690's algorithm with a 250 Hz odometry thread plus momentum-based setpoint calculation to prevent skidding in the first place. Practitioners note it is "pretty hard to use skid detection with the WPILib SwerveDrivePoseEstimator". https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/writeup-on-swerve-kinematics-and-basic-skid-detection/522622 + https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/orbit-1690s-posetracking-and-shooting-on-the-move-software-session/467814 + https://oa.pennrobotics.org/135-consul-frc-programming-framework/

**Auto-align uses a specific, non-obvious controller structure.** 6328's `DriveToPose(Drive, Supplier<Pose2d> target, Supplier<Optional<Double>> omegaOverride)` pairs a plain `PIDController` for translation with a `ProfiledPIDController` for heading, rebuilds `TrapezoidProfile.Constraints` every loop from `LoggedTunableNumber`s, and ramps feedforward in by error radius: `clamp((driveErrorAbs - linearFFMinRadius)/(linearFFMaxRadius - linearFFMinRadius), 0, 1)`. Goal detection is `withinTolerance(double driveTolerance, Rotation2d thetaTolerance)`. https://github.com/Mechanical-Advantage/RobotCode2026Public/blob/main/src/main/java/org/littletonrobotics/frc2026/commands/DriveToPose.java

**Shoot-on-the-move is an iterative time-of-flight solve that outputs setpoint *velocities*, not just positions.** 6328's 2026 `LaunchCalculator` runs a 20-iteration lookahead: apply a 30 ms phase delay, look up TOF from an interpolating map, apply an exponential drag model `(1 - exp(-TOF * dragConstant)) / dragConstant` to the launcher-relative robot velocity, offset the virtual target, and repeat. The returned `LaunchingParameters` record carries `isValid, passing, driveAngle, driveVelocity, hoodAngle, hoodVelocity, flywheelSpeed, kickerSurfaceSpeed`, plus separate map sets for normal shots (1.12–5.01 m) and passing shots (5.46–17.16 m), and trigonometric correction for an off-center launcher. https://github.com/Mechanical-Advantage/RobotCode2026Public/blob/main/src/main/java/org/littletonrobotics/frc2026/subsystems/launcher/LaunchCalculator.java

**Elite teams build tooling around the game, not just code for the game.** 6328's 2026 repo contains a `salesman/` package (`SalesmanSolver`, `SalesmanSolverIO`, `SalesmanCommands`, `SalesAssociate`) — a travelling-salesman optimizer for auto route ordering — an `energy/` package for power budgeting, `util/vts/{ChoreoJSON, ChoreoLauncher, GenerateTrajectories}` for programmatic Choreo trajectory generation, `util/LoggedTracer` for loop-time attribution, and their own `VisionIONorthstar` coprocessor pipeline. 1678's 2026 shooting package includes dedicated `verification/` and `trends/` modules, i.e. the robot grades its own shots and tracks the trend. https://github.com/Mechanical-Advantage/RobotCode2026Public + https://github.com/frc1678/C2026-Public

**Multi-camera arbitration is a real engineering problem elite teams solve explicitly.** 2910's 2025 release lists "vision relocalization with custom algorithm" including pose calculation from AprilTag data and "automatic selection of optimal camera to relocalize from" — the naive approach of feeding every camera into the estimator is not what top teams do. https://github.com/FRCTeam2910/2025CompetitionRobot-Public

**The stated bar for a 'world class software team' is process, not cleverness.** From the Feb 2026 CD thread: "If a team told me they had good unit test coverage, used tools to aid in debugging such as AdvantageKit, and could simulate their entire robot (ideally with visualization), then I'd consider them a world class software team. I just think the number of teams that do that are pretty low because none of those topics are flashy or interesting." The same thread gives the concrete FRC testing mechanics: use AdvantageKit sim IO layers for tests, step time with `SimHooks`, reset the `CommandScheduler` in `@BeforeEach`, never build the whole `RobotContainer` in one go, and move button bindings into their own class with a static setup method so the event loop can be swapped and asserted on. https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/what-should-programming-teams-really-focus-on-lessons-and-innovation-in-frc-software/513371

**Drivers are treated as the client, and 'feel' is a requirement.** From the same thread (2811 mentor): "we make sure to position our drivers as the 'clients'; Drivers say how they want the robot to operate, and coders have to make that happen. This helps prohibit certain tendencies to make singular, gross command sequences, and exposes architectural failures... Having a bot the drivers find 'feels' right is extremely valuable." This is a process practice a library can support (fast gain hot-reload, modal bindings, driver-override authority) but cannot supply. https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/what-should-programming-teams-really-focus-on-lessons-and-innovation-in-frc-software/513371

**Elite teams publish reusable configuration frameworks so code runs on more than one robot.** 3061-lib's abstract `RobotConfig` + `RobotType` enum lets one codebase drive comp bot, practice bot and sim; 2910 built a "configuration framework [that] enables running competition code on legacy robots for testing." 3061 also publishes written guides for State Machines, Tuning Odometry ("good, better, best"), Subsystem Testing and Tuning, Tuning Drivetrain and Auto, and Coordinate Systems — the pedagogy is part of the deliverable. https://github.com/HuskieRobotics/3061-lib

**Honest boundary: much of the elite advantage is NOT software.** A mentor's breakdown in the widening-gap thread lists the hard prerequisites as funding (~$13k barely built a tank-drive robot; swerve would have been ~$17k), talent pipeline and recruitment, in-house or funded 2D sheet CNC / laser cutting plus 3D printing, disciplined strategic design, a mature integrated CAD pipeline ("takes years to develop"), supplier knowledge, and — critically — a chain of ~5 subsystems minimum (up to ~10 for a top 2026 robot) that must all work: "If you screw up one you are done." No library fixes a bad drivetrain, an unreliable intake, or 3 hours of driver practice. https://www.chiefdelphi.com/t/a-look-at-the-widening-performance-gap-in-frc/516134
pitfalls: **WPILib 2027 will break everything, and it lands ~4 months from now.** roboRIO → Systemcore; Java 17 → **Java 25**; `edu.wpi.first` → **`org.wpilib`**; **Commands v3** (coroutine-based) added; `XboxController`/`PS4Controller`/etc. merged into one `Gamepad`; `MotorController.set()` → `setThrottle()`, `stopMotor()` → `disable()`; NetworkTables v3 removed; Test mode renamed Utility; Gradle 9.4.1; ZGC default; **Shuffleboard, SmartDashboard, PathWeaver and RobotBuilder deleted**; relays, analog outputs and SPI gone from hardware; and every 2026 project must be re-imported. Designing Rootstock 2026 without a 2027 plan means shipping one usable season. https://docs.wpilib.org/en/latest/docs/yearly-overview/yearly-changelog.html

**Both auto tools deliberately deferred their breaking changes to 2027.** PathPlanner 2026 has "no major changes of note... besides the addition of the 2026 field image" with the plan to "hold off on major changes for the 2027 switch to SystemCore"; Choreo 2026 "look[s] fairly similar to 2025" for the same reason. So the 2026 API stability you observe is temporary — keep the auto façade thin and never let Rootstock types leak PathPlanner/Choreo types into user-facing signatures.

**AdvantageKit replay determinism is silently breakable, and a convenience library is the most likely thing to break it.** Replay only works because every input crosses an IO boundary. Any `Timer.getFPGATimestamp()`, HAL read, `Math.random()`, background thread, or `HashMap` iteration-order dependence inside library code that is *not* behind an IO layer will make replay diverge from reality — with no error, just wrong answers. If Rootstock offers helpers that touch hardware directly, users will lose replay without knowing it. Enforce this mechanically (build-time scan) or do not claim replay support.

**The MegaTag2 heading feedback loop.** Limelight's own example calls `SetRobotOrientation(..., m_poseEstimator.getEstimatedPosition().getRotation().getDegrees(), ...)` — feeding the *fused* estimate back into the thing that produces vision measurements. This is only safe because the same example sets the rotation std dev to `9999999` (vision never affects heading). If a user (or a library) ever lowers that rotation std dev, the loop closes and the pose can walk away. Enforce gyro-only yaw structurally rather than documenting it.

**Vision timestamp error dominates on a moving robot.** At 4 m/s, a 20 ms latency/timestamp error is 8 cm of position error — larger than most teams' entire alignment tolerance. Any wrapper that resamples, buffers, or re-timestamps vision data must preserve the original capture timestamp exactly, and any `TimeInterpolatableBuffer` must be long enough (6328 uses 2.0 s) to cover worst-case coprocessor latency.

**Wheel radius drifts during an event.** Tread wear and carpet differences change the effective radius; a characterization done in the shop in January is not the number at champs. The library must make re-characterization a 60-second in-pit operation, not a code change — and should flag drift automatically by comparing odometry-only travel against vision over a match.

**Skid detection fights the pose estimator.** CD practitioners report it is "pretty hard to use skid detection with the WPILib SwerveDrivePoseEstimator," and teams still get good results without it. Implement skid as *std-dev inflation* on the odometry observation rather than a hard rejection, and ship it off by default. Also consider preventing skid instead of detecting it — Phoenix 6 2026's new `WheelForceCalculator` gives wheel-force feedforwards from robot mass and target acceleration.

**State graphs explode combinatorially.** N states means up to N² edges. 254 survives this only because edges are *auto-generated* from `allowedNextStates()` and 6328 only because edges are added in bulk over `freeNoAlgaeStates` / `freeAlgaeStates` sets. A library API that requires users to hand-enumerate edges will be abandoned at ~10 states. Generate by default; let users subtract.

**Software interlocks are not a substitute for hardware limits.** A collision rule in the state graph fails open on a disconnected encoder, a bad zero offset, or a state added without updating the rule. Elite code pairs it with forced-STOW on disable and e-stop on override (6328) — but the real backstop is motor-controller soft limits and physical hard stops. A library that markets "collision avoidance" without saying this will get someone's arm destroyed.

**Automation without a manual mode loses matches.** 254 ships `CORALMANUAL` alongside `CORAL`; 1678 keeps a second debug controller. A single-button macro that depends on vision will fail when a tag is occluded by a defender, and if there is no fallback the robot is dead for the match. Every `ScoringAction` must have a degraded manual path bound to the same physical control in another mode.

**Ordering matters: SOTM on bad odometry is worse than stopping.** Shoot-on-the-move is the flashiest 2026/2027 capability and the one small teams will want first, but it multiplies pose error into miss distance. If the pose is off by 20 cm the solver confidently aims 20 cm wrong at every distance. Gate the SOTM module behind a measured odometry-accuracy check (e.g. refuse to enable unless `OdometryReport` closure error is under a threshold).

**Over-abstraction directly contradicts 'easy to create and modify mechanisms.'** If Rootstock defines a `RootstockSubsystem` base class that mechanisms must extend, every mechanism change becomes a fight with the framework. The elite pattern is the opposite: 254 and 6328 subsystems are ordinary classes and the *coordination* layer is what is generic. Make every Rootstock layer accept plain suppliers/consumers and `Command`s so a team can adopt one piece without adopting the rest.

**Two auto DSLs is a real cognitive tax.** Supporting PathPlanner and Choreo simultaneously means students see two mental models. If the façade is not genuinely uniform, it is worse than picking one. Recommend picking Choreo as the default for time-optimal autos and PathPlanner for on-the-fly pathfinding, and document the choice rather than leaving it open.

**Log volume and roboRIO storage.** AdvantageKit records everything; the roboRIO's internal flash is not the place for it. WPILOG must go to a USB stick (`/U/logs`) and the code must degrade gracefully when the stick is missing — a robot that crashes or stalls because logging failed is a lost match. AdvantageScope 2026 added subfolder-aware log downloading precisely because log management became a chore.

**AdvantageScope custom assets drift out of sync silently.** The `Pose3d[]` you log must match `model_0.glb`, `model_1.glb`… in *count and order*. Add a component to the CAD export without updating the logged array and the visualization is quietly wrong — which then makes you distrust a correct robot. Any generator must assert consistency at build time.

**Java version trap.** The user is on Java 17 today; 2027 requires Java 25. Records, sealed interfaces and `var` are safe in 17; pattern matching for `switch` and record patterns are *preview* in 17 and must be avoided in library code that must compile on both. Pick the Java-17-safe subset now to make the 2027 port mechanical.

**CI cannot test what matters most.** GitHub Actions can run `./gradlew build test` and headless sim, but it cannot test CAN behavior, real latency, motor saturation, or a wire falling out. Teams that over-trust green CI ship confident bugs. Pair CI with the pre-match self-test (#12) which runs on real hardware.

**A library cannot fix mechanical or practice deficits, and should say so in its README.** The widening-gap thread's mentor breakdown makes the point plainly: funding, manufacturing capability, CAD maturity, supplier knowledge, and a chain of ~5–10 subsystems all working are prerequisites, and "if you screw up one you are done." Rootstock's honest claim is that it removes the *software* prerequisites — it does not remove the others.
